title: Root filesystem 100% full from a runaway application log
problem: The payments API (prod-app-03) started returning HTTP 500s and the on-call alert fired for 'disk usage > 95% on /'. New customer transactions were failing because the application could no longer write its working files, causing a partial outage of checkout.
symptoms: Application threw 'No space left on device' (ENOSPC) on every write. Users saw checkout errors. SSH still worked but commands like 'tab-completion' and creating temp files failed intermittently. Monitoring showed / at 100%.
logs:
$ df -h /
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/vg0-root   40G   40G   0G 100% /

$ tail -n 3 /var/log/app/checkout.log
2026-06-17T02:14:09Z ERROR writer: open /var/lib/app/tx/9f12.json: no space left on device
2026-06-17T02:14:09Z ERROR java.io.IOException: No space left on device

$ sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /var/log 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -4
31G  /var/log/app
31G  /var/log
420M /var/log/journal
88M  /var/log/nginx
investigationSteps: Confirmed the alert with 'df -h /' and saw Use% at 100% with 0 bytes available.
Walked the filesystem from the top with 'sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -rh | head' (using -x to stay on the root fs) and traced the bulk to /var/log.
Drilled into the directory with 'sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /var/log | sort -rh' and found /var/log/app at 31G.
Listed the offenders with 'ls -lhS /var/log/app | head' and found a single application.log at 29G that had never been rotated.
Verified the file was still actively written and held open with 'sudo lsof /var/log/app/application.log' before deciding how to reclaim space safely.
Checked whether logrotate was configured for this app with 'ls /etc/logrotate.d/' and found no entry for it.
rootCause: The application logged at DEBUG level to a single file with no rotation. A retry storm overnight amplified log volume and the unrotated application.log grew until it consumed all free space on the root filesystem.
resolution: Because the process held the file open, truncating in place (rather than rm) reclaimed space immediately without restarting the service: 'sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/app/application.log'. Confirmed recovery with 'df -h /' (Use% dropped to 31%). Then lowered the runtime log level from DEBUG to INFO and confirmed the API returned HTTP 200.
prevention: Added a logrotate rule at /etc/logrotate.d/app (daily, rotate 7, compress, copytruncate, size 200M) and validated it with 'sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/app'. Set the default app log level to INFO in config management and added a disk-usage alert threshold at 80% so the team is paged well before the filesystem fills.

title: Service fails to start after a unit/config change (missing daemon-reload)
problem: After an engineer edited the systemd unit for the internal reporting service to add an environment variable, the service would not start on deploy. The nightly report generation did not run, delaying a finance dashboard.
symptoms: 'systemctl start reporting' returned immediately but the service was not active. systemctl reported the unit was changed on disk and that systemd was using a cached version. journalctl showed the service never reached the running state.
logs:
$ sudo systemctl start reporting
Warning: The unit file, source configuration file or drop-ins of reporting.service changed on disk. Run 'systemctl daemon-reload' to reload units.

$ systemctl status reporting
* reporting.service - Nightly Reporting Service
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/reporting.service; enabled)
     Active: inactive (dead)

$ sudo journalctl -u reporting -n 5 --no-pager
-- No entries --
investigationSteps: Ran 'systemctl status reporting' and read the explicit warning that the unit file changed on disk and systemd was running a stale cached copy.
Confirmed the unit had recently been edited with 'sudo systemctl cat reporting' and 'stat /etc/systemd/system/reporting.service' to compare modification time against the last daemon-reload.
Reloaded the systemd manager configuration so it picks up the edited unit: 'sudo systemctl daemon-reload'.
Started the service again with 'sudo systemctl start reporting' and watched the result with 'systemctl status reporting'.
Tailed the journal for the unit with 'sudo journalctl -u reporting -n 30 --no-pager' to confirm it reached 'Active: active (running)' and was reading the new Environment= line.
rootCause: The unit file was edited directly under /etc/systemd/system but 'systemctl daemon-reload' was never run, so the systemd manager kept using its in-memory cached copy of the old unit and never applied the change.
resolution: Ran 'sudo systemctl daemon-reload' to reload unit definitions, then 'sudo systemctl restart reporting'. Verified with 'systemctl status reporting' that it was active and running, and confirmed the new environment variable was present using 'systemctl show reporting -p Environment'.
prevention: Updated the deploy runbook and CI deploy script so any change to a unit file is always followed by 'systemctl daemon-reload' before start/restart. Added a post-deploy smoke check that asserts the service is 'active' and fails the pipeline otherwise.

title: OOM killer terminated the application process
problem: The catalog search service (prod-search-01) disappeared without an orderly shutdown and search returned errors site-wide. The process exited with no application-level error in its own logs, suggesting it was killed externally.
symptoms: The Java process vanished and systemd showed it as failed with a non-zero status. The application's own log just stopped mid-request. Available memory had been trending down for hours before the kill.
logs:
$ systemctl status search
* search.service - Catalog Search
     Active: failed (Result: signal) since Wed 2026-06-17 03:41:22 UTC
    Process: 2031 ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/search/search.jar (code=killed, signal=KILL)

$ sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'killed process|out of memory' | tail -3
[Wed Jun 17 03:41:22 2026] Out of memory: Killed process 2031 (java) total-vm:8123944kB, anon-rss:6995112kB, file-rss:0kB, oom_score_adj:0

$ sudo journalctl -k -n 4 --no-pager
Jun 17 03:41:22 prod-search-01 kernel: oom-kill:constraint=CONSTRAINT_NONE,nodemask=(null),cpuset=/,mems_allowed=0,global_oom,task=java,pid=2031
Jun 17 03:41:22 prod-search-01 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 2031 (java)
investigationSteps: Saw the service in 'failed (Result: signal)' state via 'systemctl status search' and noted 'code=killed, signal=KILL' which points to an external kill, not an app crash.
Confirmed it was the kernel OOM killer with 'sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E "killed process|out of memory"' and found the 'Out of memory: Killed process 2031 (java)' line.
Cross-checked the kernel ring buffer in the journal with 'sudo journalctl -k --since "04:00" | grep -i oom' to capture the oom-kill constraint and the rss size at time of death.
Reviewed overall memory with 'free -h' and per-process usage with 'ps aux --sort=-%mem | head' to see the JVM's resident set had grown far beyond its intended heap.
Inspected the launch command and JVM flags with 'systemctl cat search' and found no -Xmx cap, so the heap was allowed to grow toward physical RAM.
Reviewed historical memory metrics in the monitoring dashboard to confirm a steady climb (a leak/unbounded cache) rather than a sudden spike.
rootCause: The JVM was started without a maximum heap limit (-Xmx) and an unbounded in-memory result cache grew until the JVM's resident set exceeded available RAM. With no swap headroom, the kernel OOM killer selected the largest task (the java process) and sent SIGKILL.
resolution: Restarted the service to restore search immediately with 'sudo systemctl restart search'. Set an explicit heap cap by adding '-Xmx4g' to ExecStart, ran 'sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart search', and verified the new limit with 'ps -o pid,rss,args -C java'. Confirmed search returned results and memory stabilized via 'free -h'.
prevention: Bounded the application cache size in config, added a JVM heap alert and an OS memory alert at 85%, and added a small swap file as a safety margin. Filed a ticket to investigate the suspected cache leak and added a periodic heap usage check to monitoring.

title: High CPU pinned at 100% from a runaway cron-spawned process
problem: Monitoring alerted that prod-batch-02 had load average above 30 on a 4-core box and the web app on the same host became sluggish. Response times degraded for end users sharing the server's CPU.
symptoms: Load average was an order of magnitude above the core count and one process sat at ~100% CPU continuously. The system was responsive to SSH but every interactive command was slow. The CPU spike began on the hour.
logs:
$ uptime
 03:55:14 up 12 days,  load average: 31.20, 28.04, 19.77

$ top -b -n1 | head -12
top - 03:55:16 up 12 days,  load average: 31.20, 28.04, 19.77
%Cpu(s): 99.7 us,  0.3 sy,  0.0 ni,  0.0 id
  PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND
 6620 batch     20   0  118400   9300   2400 R  99.3  0.1  41:12.88 process_feed.sh
 6621 batch     20   0    9200   2100   1800 R   0.7  0.0   0:00.40 grep

$ ps -o pid,ppid,etime,cmd -p 6620
  PID  PPID     ELAPSED CMD
 6620  6500    00:41:12 /bin/bash /opt/batch/process_feed.sh
investigationSteps: Confirmed the high load with 'uptime' (load 31 on a 4-core host) and 'nproc' to know the core count.
Identified the single hottest process with 'top -b -n1' (sorted by CPU), spotting process_feed.sh pinned at ~99% in state R.
Traced the process's parent and runtime with 'ps -o pid,ppid,etime,cmd -p 6620', noting it had run far longer than its expected few seconds and its parent was a cron-launched shell.
Confirmed cron started it with 'grep CRON /var/log/syslog | tail' and matched the PPID to the hourly cron entry in 'crontab -l -u batch'.
Read the script and found a 'while' loop polling a feed file that, when the feed was missing, never satisfied its exit condition and span without any sleep.
Captured a quick CPU profile with 'pidstat -p 6620 1 3' to confirm it was burning user CPU in a tight loop rather than waiting on I/O.
rootCause: An hourly cron job ran process_feed.sh, which contained a 'while [ ! -f $FEED ]' busy-wait loop with no sleep. The upstream feed failed to arrive, so the loop never exited and consumed a full core; successive hourly runs would have stacked more.
resolution: Stopped the runaway process immediately with 'sudo kill 6620' (and confirmed it was gone with 'ps -p 6620'), which dropped load back toward normal. Edited the script to add a bounded retry with 'sleep 5' and a max attempt count that exits non-zero, so a missing feed fails fast instead of spinning.
prevention: Wrapped cron-driven scripts with a runtime guard (timeout 300 ...) and added flock to prevent overlapping runs from stacking. Added a CPU/load alert and a check that the upstream feed exists before processing, alerting if it is missing rather than busy-waiting.

title: 'Permission denied' running a script after a deploy (wrong owner/mode)
problem: After a new release was rolled out, the application service failed to start and the deploy pipeline marked the host unhealthy. The startup wrapper script could not be executed, blocking the release on prod-api-04.
symptoms: systemd reported the unit failed with status 203/EXEC. Running the wrapper script by hand returned 'Permission denied'. The files existed and looked correct in 'ls' except the execute bit was missing and ownership was root instead of the service account.
logs:
$ systemctl status api
* api.service - API Service
     Active: failed (Result: exit-code)
    Process: 4810 ExecStart=/opt/api/bin/start.sh (code=exited, status=203/EXEC)

$ sudo journalctl -u api -n 3 --no-pager
Jun 17 09:02:11 prod-api-04 systemd[1]: api.service: Failed to execute /opt/api/bin/start.sh: Permission denied
Jun 17 09:02:11 prod-api-04 systemd[1]: api.service: Failed at step EXEC spawning /opt/api/bin/start.sh: Permission denied

$ ls -l /opt/api/bin/start.sh
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 412 Jun 17 09:01 /opt/api/bin/start.sh

$ sudo -u apiuser /opt/api/bin/start.sh
bash: /opt/api/bin/start.sh: Permission denied
investigationSteps: Read 'systemctl status api' and recognized status=203/EXEC, which systemd uses specifically when it cannot execute the ExecStart binary.
Confirmed the exact failure with 'sudo journalctl -u api -n 20 --no-pager' showing 'Failed to execute ... : Permission denied' at the EXEC step.
Inspected the file with 'ls -l /opt/api/bin/start.sh' and saw mode -rw-r--r-- (no execute bit) and owner root:root instead of apiuser.
Reproduced the failure as the service account with 'sudo -u apiuser /opt/api/bin/start.sh' to confirm it was a permission/ownership problem and not a bad shebang.
Checked the interpreter line with 'head -1 /opt/api/bin/start.sh' to rule out a missing or wrong shebang as a second cause.
rootCause: The deploy step extracted the release as root and did not restore the execute bit or service-account ownership, so the script landed as root:root mode 644. systemd could not exec a non-executable file owned by another user and failed with 203/EXEC.
resolution: Restored ownership and the execute bit: 'sudo chown apiuser:apiuser /opt/api/bin/start.sh' and 'sudo chmod 750 /opt/api/bin/start.sh'. Re-ran the service with 'sudo systemctl start api' and confirmed 'Active: active (running)' via 'systemctl status api'.
prevention: Fixed the deploy artifact so permissions are baked into the package (tar preserves mode) and added an explicit 'chmod +x' and 'chown' step in the post-extract hook. Added a deploy smoke test that runs 'test -x /opt/api/bin/start.sh' and fails the rollout if the bit is missing.

title: Disk full but du can't find the space (deleted-but-open file held by a process)
problem: prod-log-01 alerted at 98% on /var, but the team could not locate the large files: 'du' on /var added up to far less than what 'df' reported as used. Log ingestion began failing because the partition was nearly full, risking loss of audit data.
symptoms: 'df -h /var' showed ~96% used while 'du -sh /var' summed to only a fraction of that. Deleting old files in the directory did not free space. The gap between df and du was several gigabytes and growing.
logs:
$ df -h /var
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sdb1        50G   48G  2.0G  96% /var

$ sudo du -sh /var
19G  /var

$ sudo lsof +L1 | head -6
COMMAND   PID  USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE  SIZE/OFF NLINK  NODE NAME
rsyslogd  988  root    7w  REG    8,17 28991029248     0 26214 /var/log/old-debug.log (deleted)
java      2210 app     142w REG   8,17  3221225472     0 26890 /var/lib/app/tmp/buffer.bin (deleted)

$ sudo ls -l /proc/988/fd/7
l-wx------ 1 root root 64 Jun 17 10:30 /proc/988/fd/7 -> /var/log/old-debug.log (deleted)
investigationSteps: Confirmed the contradiction directly: 'df -h /var' reported 96% used but 'sudo du -sh /var' summed to ~19G, a large unexplained gap.
Recognized the classic signature of a deleted-but-still-open file (space not freed until the holding process closes the descriptor or exits).
Listed open files with a positive size whose link count is zero using 'sudo lsof +L1', which surfaces files marked '(deleted)' still held open.
Identified the worst offender as rsyslogd PID 988 holding /var/log/old-debug.log (deleted) at ~27G via the lsof NLINK 0 entry.
Confirmed the held descriptor through procfs with 'sudo ls -l /proc/988/fd/7' showing the symlink target marked '(deleted)'.
Decided on the safest reclaim path: free the descriptor without losing the running service, choosing to truncate via the procfs fd rather than restart blindly.
rootCause: An operator had 'rm'd an old debug log while rsyslogd still had it open. On Linux, unlinking a file does not free its blocks until every open file descriptor is closed, so rsyslogd kept the deleted file's 27G allocated even though the path no longer appeared in 'du'.
resolution: Reclaimed the space without dropping the service by truncating through the open descriptor in procfs: 'sudo truncate -s 0 /proc/988/fd/7'. Confirmed recovery with 'df -h /var' (used dropped to ~21G). For the secondary java buffer, a graceful 'sudo systemctl restart app' released its deleted file too. Verified log ingestion resumed.
prevention: Documented that operators must truncate or rotate logs (logrotate with copytruncate) rather than 'rm' files held open by daemons. Added a monitoring check that compares df vs du and a periodic 'lsof +L1' audit to catch deleted-but-open files early. Configured proper rotation for rsyslog.

title: Cron job silently didn't run overnight (PATH / exec bit / MAILTO)
problem: The nightly database backup that runs from cron did not produce a file overnight, and nobody received an error. The most recent backup was 26 hours old, breaching the recovery point objective for the reporting database.
symptoms: No new dump appeared in the backup directory. The cron job produced no email and no obvious error. cron logs showed the job was launched on schedule, yet it produced no output and the script exited almost immediately.
logs:
$ ls -l --time-style=+%Y-%m-%d /backups | tail -2
-rw-r--r-- 1 dbops dbops 1043M 2026-06-15 db_dump_20260615.sql.gz
-rw-r--r-- 1 dbops dbops 1041M 2026-06-16 db_dump_20260616.sql.gz

$ grep CRON /var/log/syslog | grep backup | tail -2
Jun 17 02:00:01 prod-db-01 CRON[7781]: (dbops) CMD (/opt/backup/run_backup.sh)
Jun 17 02:00:01 prod-db-01 CRON[7780]: (CRON) info (No MTA installed, discarding output)

$ crontab -l -u dbops
0 2 * * * /opt/backup/run_backup.sh

$ sudo -u dbops -i /opt/backup/run_backup.sh; echo "exit=$?"
/opt/backup/run_backup.sh: line 8: pg_dump: command not found
exit=127
investigationSteps: Confirmed the missing artifact with 'ls -l /backups' and noted the newest dump was from two days prior.
Verified cron actually launched the job by checking 'grep CRON /var/log/syslog | grep backup', which showed the scheduled CMD line at 02:00.
Spotted the 'No MTA installed, discarding output' message, explaining why no failure email arrived and why the error was silent.
Read the crontab with 'crontab -l -u dbops' to confirm the schedule and the exact command path.
Reproduced the job in a cron-like minimal environment with 'sudo -u dbops -i /opt/backup/run_backup.sh; echo exit=$?' and got 'pg_dump: command not found' with exit 127.
Compared interactive PATH ('echo $PATH') with cron's limited PATH and confirmed pg_dump lived in /usr/pgsql-15/bin, which is not on cron's default PATH.
rootCause: The backup script called 'pg_dump' by bare name. cron runs with a minimal PATH (typically /usr/bin:/bin) that does not include /usr/pgsql-15/bin, so pg_dump was not found and the script exited 127. Because no MTA was installed, cron's output (the error) was silently discarded, so the failure went unnoticed.
resolution: Fixed the script to use the absolute path '/usr/pgsql-15/bin/pg_dump' (and set an explicit PATH at the top of the script). Re-ran it under the service account to confirm a fresh dump was produced and exit code 0. Took an immediate manual backup to close the RPO gap.
prevention: Set MAILTO and installed a lightweight MTA (or redirect cron output to a logged file and alert on it) so failures are never silent. Standardized on absolute binary paths or an explicit PATH line in cron scripts. Added a monitoring check that alerts if the newest backup file is older than 24 hours.

title: Inode exhaustion (df shows space free but writes fail) from millions of small files
problem: The mail/session host prod-sess-02 began rejecting new writes with 'No space left on device' even though 'df -h' showed plenty of free gigabytes. New user sessions could not be created, intermittently locking customers out.
symptoms: Applications failed to create files with ENOSPC, yet 'df -h' reported the filesystem only ~40% used by size. The failures correlated with a directory that had accumulated an enormous number of tiny session files. 'df -i' told a very different story from 'df -h'.
logs:
$ df -h /var
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sdc1       80G   31G   49G  40% /var

$ touch /var/lib/sessions/test
touch: cannot touch '/var/lib/sessions/test': No space left on device

$ df -i /var
Filesystem      Inodes   IUsed IFree IUse% Mounted on
/dev/sdc1     5242880 5242871     9   100% /var

$ for d in /var/lib/sessions/*/; do echo "$(find "$d" -xdev | wc -l) $d"; done | sort -rn | head -3
4988120 /var/lib/sessions/cache/
201233 /var/lib/sessions/active/
982 /var/lib/sessions/locks/
investigationSteps: Saw the paradox: writes failed with ENOSPC but 'df -h /var' showed 49G free, so size was not the limit.
Reproduced the failure cheaply with 'touch /var/lib/sessions/test' to confirm even a zero-byte create failed.
Checked inode usage with 'df -i /var' and found IUse% at 100% (5.24M inodes used) — the filesystem was out of inodes, not bytes.
Located which directory consumed the inodes by counting entries per subtree with a 'find ... | wc -l' loop, isolating /var/lib/sessions/cache with ~5 million tiny files.
Confirmed the files were stale, orphaned session blobs that a cleanup job should have removed, by checking their ages with 'find /var/lib/sessions/cache -type f -mtime +2 | head' and 'ls -l'.
Verified the cleanup cron that should prune them and found it had been failing (separate issue), allowing files to accumulate without bound.
rootCause: A session cache directory accumulated roughly 5 million tiny files because the pruning job was not removing them. Each file consumes one inode; the ext4 filesystem was formatted with a fixed inode count that became exhausted while plenty of byte capacity remained, so all creates failed with ENOSPC.
resolution: Freed inodes by deleting the stale files in a way that scales to millions of entries: 'sudo find /var/lib/sessions/cache -type f -mtime +1 -delete' (using find -delete to avoid argument-list overflow that 'rm *' hits). Confirmed recovery with 'df -i /var' (IUse% dropped well below 100%) and verified 'touch' succeeded again.
prevention: Fixed and re-enabled the cleanup cron, and added a tmpreaper/systemd-tmpfiles rule to age out session files automatically. Added a 'df -i' inode-usage alert at 80% (size alerts alone would never have caught this). Recommended sharding session files into subdirectories and considering a filesystem with dynamic inodes (XFS) for this workload.

title: Server very slow due to memory pressure and heavy swapping
problem: Users reported the analytics host prod-analytics-01 had become extremely sluggish; page loads and queries that normally took under a second were taking many seconds. The box was not down, but throughput collapsed during the business day.
symptoms: High I/O wait and constant disk activity even though the workload was CPU/memory bound, not disk bound. 'free -h' showed almost no free memory and swap heavily used. Latency spiked whenever memory pressure rose, indicating the system was thrashing.
logs:
$ free -h
              total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           15Gi        14Gi       180Mi        12Mi       900Mi       210Mi
Swap:         4.0Gi       3.9Gi       110Mi

$ vmstat 1 4
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
 5  3 4087800 184320  20480 901120 5120 6144  6200  7100 3200 5400 22  9  3 66  0
 4  4 4090112 180224  20480 900096 6400 7168  7000  7900 3500 5800 20 10  2 68  0

$ ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -3
USER  PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS COMMAND
analy 3120 18.0 61.2 9876544 9600000 /usr/bin/python3 /opt/etl/aggregate.py
analy 3144 12.0 21.5 3800000 3370000 /usr/bin/python3 /opt/etl/loader.py
investigationSteps: Checked memory headroom with 'free -h' and saw 'available' at ~210Mi and swap almost fully consumed (3.9Gi of 4Gi).
Ran 'vmstat 1' and saw sustained non-zero 'si'/'so' (swap-in/swap-out) every second plus high 'wa' (~66%), the textbook signature of thrashing.
Confirmed the disk activity was paging, not application I/O, by correlating the swap columns with iostat ('iostat -xz 1') showing the swap device busy.
Identified the memory hog with 'ps aux --sort=-%mem | head' and found aggregate.py holding ~9.6G RSS (61% of RAM).
Reviewed the ETL job and found it loaded an entire dataset into a Python list in memory instead of streaming, and that two ETL jobs had been scheduled to overlap.
Checked 'cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness' and recent capacity trends to decide between a quick mitigation (stop the overlapping job) and a real fix (bound memory).
rootCause: An ETL aggregation job loaded a large dataset fully into memory and was scheduled to overlap with a second ETL job. Combined resident memory exceeded physical RAM, so the kernel paged heavily to swap; the resulting swap-in/swap-out thrashing dominated the disk and starved every process of CPU time, making the whole host slow.
resolution: Relieved pressure immediately by stopping the overlapping job ('sudo systemctl stop etl-loader') so working set fit in RAM; swap drained and latency recovered within minutes (confirmed via 'free -h' and 'vmstat 1'). Refactored aggregate.py to stream/iterate in chunks instead of loading everything, and rescheduled the two ETL jobs so they no longer overlap.
prevention: Added memory and swap-usage alerts (and a 'vmstat si/so' check) so thrashing pages the team before users notice. Put the ETL jobs under systemd with MemoryMax= cgroup limits so a runaway job is constrained rather than swapping the host. Reviewed RAM sizing for the workload and serialized the ETL schedule.

title: Users can't SSH in / sudo fails after /tmp filled and disk pressure
problem: Multiple engineers suddenly could not establish new SSH sessions to prod-jump-01, and the few who were still logged in found 'sudo' failing. With the jump host inaccessible, the team lost their path to manage downstream production servers.
symptoms: New SSH logins hung or closed immediately after authentication. On an existing session, 'sudo' returned errors and PAM logged session-open failures. The root filesystem and /tmp were full, and writing the lastlog/utmp and creating session files failed.
logs:
$ ssh prod-jump-01
... (authentication succeeds, then) ...
Connection to prod-jump-01 closed.

# from the one remaining live session:
$ df -h / /tmp
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/vda1        20G   20G    0G 100% /

$ sudo systemctl status sshd
sudo: unable to open /var/lib/sudo/ts/eng01: No space left on device
sudo: error initializing audit plugin

$ sudo journalctl -u sshd -n 4 --no-pager
Jun 17 14:05:01 prod-jump-01 sshd[5521]: pam_systemd(sshd:session): Failed to create session: No space left on device
Jun 17 14:05:01 prod-jump-01 sshd[5521]: error: PAM: pam_open_session: System error
investigationSteps: From the single still-connected session, ran 'df -h / /tmp' and found both at 100% used with 0 bytes free — the root cause class was disk-full, not sshd config.

Correlated the symptoms: read 'sudo journalctl -u sshd' and saw 'pam_open_session: System error' and 'Failed to create session: No space left on device', explaining why new logins dropped right after auth.
Noted that 'sudo' itself failed with 'unable to open /var/lib/sudo/ts/...: No space left on device', tying sudo failure to the same full filesystem.
Found the space consumer with 'sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -rh | head' and traced the bulk to /tmp full of large stale upload files left by a batch process.
Confirmed nothing critical was holding those temp files open with a quick 'sudo lsof /tmp/<file>' check before deleting, then reclaimed space.
After freeing space, validated that a brand-new SSH session and 'sudo' both worked, and checked 'systemctl status sshd' was healthy.
rootCause: A batch process wrote large temporary files into /tmp and never cleaned them up, filling the root filesystem to 100%. With zero free space, PAM/systemd could not create new login sessions (it needs to write session and lastlog/utmp data) and sudo could not write its timestamp/audit files, so new SSH logins were dropped after authentication and sudo failed.
resolution: Reclaimed space from the live session by removing the stale temp files: 'sudo find /tmp -type f -mtime +1 -size +50M -delete'. Confirmed free space returned with 'df -h /'. New SSH sessions and sudo immediately started working again. No sshd restart was required once disk space was available.
prevention: Added a systemd-tmpfiles policy to age out /tmp automatically and fixed the batch process to clean up its temp files. Added a disk-usage alert at 80% on the jump host and configured a small dedicated /tmp (or tmpfs with a size cap) so a temp-file flood cannot fill the root filesystem and lock out logins. Documented an out-of-band console access path for when SSH is unavailable.

title: Order lookup endpoint slow due to full table scan on missing index
problem: The customer-facing 'My Orders' page started timing out for some users. Latency on the orders API rose from ~40ms to 2-6 seconds, and support tickets reported the page 'hanging' at peak hours.
symptoms: p95 latency on GET /api/orders spiked; APM showed a single query dominating wall time; CPU on the primary climbed to 85%+ during business hours; the slowness scaled with the size of the orders table (worse over time).
logs:
# MySQL slow query log
# Time: 2026-06-15T13:22:41.118Z
# Query_time: 4.812  Lock_time: 0.000  Rows_sent: 18  Rows_examined: 2841190
SELECT id, total_cents, status, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 90421 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 25;

mysql> EXPLAIN SELECT id, total_cents, status, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 90421 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 25;
+----+-------------+--------+------+---------------+------+---------+------+---------+-----------------------------+
| id | select_type | table  | type | possible_keys | key  | key_len | ref  | rows    | Extra                       |
+----+-------------+--------+------+---------------+------+---------+------+---------+-----------------------------+
|  1 | SIMPLE      | orders | ALL  | NULL          | NULL | NULL    | NULL | 2841190 | Using where; Using filesort |
+----+-------------+--------+------+---------------+------+---------+------+---------+-----------------------------+
investigationSteps: Enabled/inspected the slow query log: SET GLOBAL slow_query_log=ON; SET GLOBAL long_query_time=1; then tailed the log to find the worst offenders by Query_time and Rows_examined.
Ran EXPLAIN on the offending query and saw type=ALL (full table scan), key=NULL, and rows ~2.8M with 'Using filesort', confirming no usable index.
Checked existing indexes with SHOW INDEX FROM orders; only PRIMARY (id) existed — no index on customer_id.
Estimated selectivity: SELECT COUNT(*) , COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders; confirmed customer_id is highly selective (good index candidate).
Validated the fix on a staging copy by adding a composite index and re-running EXPLAIN to confirm the plan changed before touching production.
rootCause: The orders table had no index on customer_id (and none supporting the created_at sort). As the table grew past ~2.8M rows, every per-customer lookup performed a full table scan plus a filesort, so latency grew linearly with table size.
resolution: Added a composite index matching the WHERE + ORDER BY: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC); Used ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE on MySQL 8 to avoid blocking writes. After the index, EXPLAIN showed type=ref, key=idx_orders_customer_created, rows~18, and 'Using filesort' disappeared; query time dropped to ~3ms.
prevention: Add an index-review gate to schema migrations; enable the slow query log permanently with long_query_time=1 and alert on Rows_examined/Rows_sent ratio; run pt-query-digest weekly; require EXPLAIN output in PRs for any new query against large tables.

title: Checkout writes failing with 'Lock wait timeout exceeded' from a deadlock-prone update order
problem: During a flash sale, checkout requests began failing intermittently with HTTP 500s. The application surfaced 'Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction', and a portion of orders failed to commit, directly impacting revenue.
symptoms: Bursts of failed checkouts correlated with traffic spikes; some transactions hung for ~50s then errored; InnoDB row-lock waits and deadlock counters climbed; the inventory and orders tables were the hotspots.
logs:
ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction

------------------------

*** (1) TRANSACTION:
TRANSACTION 84412199, ACTIVE 9 sec starting index read
mysql tables in use 1, locked 1
LOCK WAIT 4 lock struct(s), heap size 1136, 2 row lock(s)

investigationSteps: Reproduced under load and captured SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G; read the 'LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK' section to identify the two transactions and the rows they each held vs waited on.
Listed live waits via SHOW PROCESSLIST and the data dictionary: SELECT * FROM performance_schema.data_lock_waits; joined to data_locks to see blocking vs blocked threads.
Confirmed the timeout threshold: SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_lock_wait_timeout'; (default 50s) explained the ~50s hangs before failure.

Reviewed the checkout transaction in code and found multi-row inventory updates issued in differing SKU order across requests, plus an external payment API call made while the transaction was open (holding locks for seconds).
Confirmed lock ordering hypothesis by tracing two concurrent carts updating SKUs 5567 and 5531 in opposite sequence — the classic AB/BA deadlock.
rootCause: Two issues compounded: (1) the application updated multiple inventory rows in inconsistent SKU order across concurrent transactions, creating circular lock dependencies (deadlocks); (2) a slow external payment call was executed inside the open transaction, holding row locks long enough to push waiters past innodb_lock_wait_timeout.
resolution: Enforced a deterministic lock order by sorting SKUs ascending before updating (ORDER BY sku_id) so all transactions acquire locks in the same sequence. Moved the payment API call outside the DB transaction (authorize first, then a short transaction to decrement inventory and insert the order). Added application-level retry-on-deadlock (retry up to 3x on errors 1205/1213 with jitter). Verified with SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS that deadlocks dropped to zero under the same load.
prevention: Keep transactions short and never call external services inside them; always acquire locks in a consistent order; implement idempotent retry on 1205/1213; monitor Innodb_row_lock_time_avg and deadlock counts; load-test checkout concurrency before sale events.

title: Stale reads after checkout caused by read-replica replication lag
problem: Customers reported that immediately after placing an order, the order did not appear on their order history, and account balances looked outdated for several seconds to minutes. No data was lost, but the inconsistency generated duplicate-order complaints.
symptoms: Reads served from the replica returned pre-write state; the lag spiked during a nightly batch job and during a large bulk price update; writes on the primary were fine; the gap closed on its own once replication caught up.
logs:
mysql> SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
*************************** 1. row ***************************
          Replica_IO_Running: Yes
         Replica_SQL_Running: Yes
      Seconds_Behind_Source: 214
              Source_Log_File: mysql-bin.000231
          Read_Source_Log_Pos: 884221190
               Relay_Log_File: relay-bin.000119
                Relay_Log_Pos: 12044
        Source_Log_File: mysql-bin.000233
      Exec_Source_Log_Pos: 511002233
   Replica_SQL_Running_State: Reading event from the relay log

# pt-heartbeat sample on replica
2026-06-15T02:41:00  delay=212s  host=replica-1
investigationSteps: Quantified lag with SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G and the more reliable pt-heartbeat delay metric; confirmed Seconds_Behind_Source spiked to ~3.5 min during the nightly job.
Verified threads were healthy (Replica_IO_Running=Yes, Replica_SQL_Running=Yes) so this was apply lag, not a broken replica.
Checked whether the SQL apply was single-threaded: SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'replica_parallel_workers'; found it set to 0 (serial apply), bottlenecking on large transactions.
Correlated lag windows with the workload: identified a bulk UPDATE on products and a large nightly ETL writing huge single transactions on the primary.
Reviewed application read routing and confirmed read-after-write paths (order confirmation, balance) were being sent to the replica with no consistency guarantee.
rootCause: The replica applied relay logs single-threaded, so large transactions on the primary (bulk price update, nightly ETL) created multi-minute apply lag. The application routed read-after-write queries to the lagging replica, so users saw stale state right after their own writes.
resolution: Enabled multithreaded apply: SET GLOBAL replica_parallel_workers=4; SET GLOBAL replica_parallel_type='LOGICAL_CLOCK'; and persisted it in my.cnf. Broke the bulk update and ETL into smaller batched transactions to reduce per-transaction apply time. Routed read-after-write-sensitive queries (order confirmation, balances) to the primary, and for others used MASTER_POS_WAIT()/WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET to wait for the write to replicate before reading. Lag dropped to <2s.
prevention: Alert on Seconds_Behind_Source / pt-heartbeat delay above a threshold; keep replica_parallel_workers tuned; batch large writes; adopt explicit read-after-write consistency (route critical reads to primary or wait on GTID); avoid huge single-transaction ETL on the primary.

title: App outage from 'Too many connections' due to a leaked connection pool
problem: The application went fully down with database connection errors. Every new request failed with 'Too many connections', causing a complete service outage until connections were cleared.
symptoms: Errors began gradually then hit a wall once the cap was reached; the connection count climbed steadily over hours and never dropped; most connections sat in 'Sleep' state for a long time; a recent deploy of a reporting feature preceded the issue.
logs:
ERROR 1040 (HY000): Too many connections

mysql> SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Threads_connected';
+-------------------+-------+
| Variable_name     | Value |
+-------------------+-------+
| Threads_connected | 151   |
+-------------------+-------+
mysql> SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_connections';
+-----------------+-------+
| Variable_name   | Value |
+-----------------+-------+
| max_connections | 151   |
+-----------------+-------+

mysql> SELECT user, COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.processlist GROUP BY user ORDER BY 2 DESC;
+-----------+----------+
| user      | COUNT(*) |
+-----------+----------+
| app_svc   |      146 |
| root      |        2 |
+-----------+----------+
# Most app_svc threads: Command=Sleep, Time=3400+
investigationSteps: Confirmed the cap was hit: SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Threads_connected'; equaled SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_connections'; (151).
Inspected SHOW PROCESSLIST / information_schema.processlist and saw ~146 connections from app_svc, almost all Command=Sleep with very high Time — idle, not running queries.
Trended connections over time via monitoring and saw a monotonic climb with no release, ruling out a legitimate traffic spike and pointing to a leak.

Correlated the onset with the recent reporting-feature deploy; reviewed the new code path and found connections opened for ad-hoc reports were never returned to the pool on the exception path (missing close/try-with-resources).
Checked the pool config and found maxPoolSize larger than the server's max_connections and no idle/leak timeout configured.
rootCause: A new reporting code path acquired database connections but failed to release them on error paths, leaking connections back to neither the pool nor the server. Combined with a pool max larger than the server's max_connections and no leak/idle timeout, idle 'Sleep' connections accumulated until the server hit max_connections and refused all new connections.
resolution: Immediate relief: raised the cap briefly (SET GLOBAL max_connections=300;) and killed stale sleepers (built KILL statements from SELECT id FROM information_schema.processlist WHERE command='Sleep' AND time>600 AND user='app_svc';) to restore service. Permanent fix: wrapped connection usage in try-with-resources to guarantee release, set the pool maxPoolSize below the server cap, and configured idle and leak-detection timeouts (e.g., HikariCP idleTimeout and leakDetectionThreshold). Also set a server-side wait_timeout so abandoned connections eventually close.
prevention: Always release connections in finally/try-with-resources; size pool maxPoolSize < max_connections with headroom for admin; enable pool leak detection and idle timeout; set server wait_timeout/interactive_timeout; alert when Threads_connected approaches max_connections; smoke-test new DB code paths for leaks before deploy.

title: MySQL service won't start after host reboot — port already in use plus disk full
problem: After a maintenance reboot, the MySQL service failed to start and the database was completely unavailable. The application could not connect at all, taking the dependent services down.
symptoms: systemctl start mysql exited non-zero and the service flapped in auto-restart; the error log showed a bind/address-in-use failure on the first attempt; after that was cleared, startup then failed writing to disk; df reported the data volume at 100%.
logs:

2026-06-14T08:12:03Z [ERROR] [MY-010119] [Server] Aborting
... (after killing stray process) ...
2026-06-14T08:19:41Z [ERROR] [MY-012574] [InnoDB] Unable to allocate ... 
2026-06-14T08:19:41Z [ERROR] [MY-012592] [InnoDB] Operating system error number 28 in a file operation.
2026-06-14T08:19:41Z [ERROR] [MY-011825] [InnoDB] Error 28 means 'No space left on device'
2026-06-14T08:19:41Z [ERROR] [InnoDB] Could not open or create the system tablespace.

$ df -h /var/lib/mysql
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/nvme1n1    100G  100G     0 100% /var/lib/mysql
investigationSteps: Read the MySQL error log first (/var/log/mysql/error.log) to get the actual failure rather than guessing from systemd's generic message.
Diagnosed the first error (Address already in use) with sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :3306' and found a stray/zombie mysqld holding port 3306 after the unclean shutdown.
Cleared the stale process (confirmed it was the old mysqld, then terminated it) and retried start, which exposed the next error.
Saw InnoDB OS error 28 'No space left on device' and ran df -h /var/lib/mysql to confirm the data volume was 100% full.
Found the space consumer with du -xh --max-depth=1 /var/lib/mysql | sort -h and identified bloated binary logs and a large slow/general log as the main offenders.

Freed space safely (purged old binary logs, rotated/truncated the oversized log files — not the data files), confirmed free space with df, then started MySQL cleanly and validated with SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS and a test query.
rootCause: Two stacked failures: an unclean shutdown left a stray mysqld holding TCP port 3306 (Address already in use), and the data volume had filled to 100% (mostly from unpurged binary logs and oversized log files), so InnoDB could not write the system tablespace and aborted with OS error 28.
resolution: Freed the port by terminating the stale mysqld found via ss -ltnp. Freed disk by purging old binary logs and rotating logs: PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE '2026-06-10 00:00:00'; (run once DB was up) plus removing/rotating the bloated /var/log/mysql files; confirmed df showed free space. Started the service (systemctl start mysql), verified clean startup in the error log, and confirmed connectivity and InnoDB recovery completed.
prevention: Set binlog auto-expiry (binlog_expire_logs_seconds, e.g. 7 days) and log rotation via logrotate; put binary/general/slow logs on monitored, alertable disk usage (alert at 80%); ensure clean shutdown ordering on reboot (systemd dependency / ExecStop); add a startup health check that verifies free space and port availability.

title: Accidental UPDATE without WHERE overwrote every row — point-in-time recovery via backup + binlog
problem: An operator ran an UPDATE in production without a WHERE clause, setting the same value on every row of the customers table. All customer email-preference and tier values were overwritten, corrupting data for the entire customer base.
symptoms: Rows_matched equaled the full table count in the client output; the app immediately showed every customer with identical (wrong) values; no application bug — a single human-issued statement caused mass corruption; the exact statement and timestamp were recoverable from the binary log.
investigationSteps: Stopped the bleeding first: revoked write access / put the affected table into read-only handling and notified stakeholders to prevent further changes and overwriting of recoverable data.

Located the exact bad event and its timestamp/position in the binary logs using mysqlbinlog --base64-output=DECODE-ROWS -v, confirming server time 2026-06-16 14:52:10 just before binlog position 774120355.
Identified the most recent good full backup (logical dump taken at 02:00:00) and confirmed binary logging was enabled continuously since the backup so PITR was possible.
Restored the full backup into an isolated recovery instance (not production) to rebuild the table at the backup point without risking live data.

Replayed binary logs onto the recovery instance from the backup position up to just before the bad statement: mysqlbinlog --start-position=<backup_pos> --stop-datetime='2026-06-16 14:52:10' mysql-bin.0002* | mysql, reconstructing the table to its state one second before the mistake.

Validated the recovered customers table (row counts, spot-checks of tier values for known accounts) against expectations, then swapped/loaded the corrected table back into production during a short maintenance window.
rootCause: A human-issued UPDATE statement omitted the WHERE clause, so it matched and changed all 482,113 rows. Operating in a session without safe-update protection (sql_safe_updates off) allowed the unfiltered mass update to execute.
resolution: Performed point-in-time recovery: restored the 02:00 full backup to a recovery instance, then applied binary logs with mysqlbinlog up to --stop-datetime just before 14:52:10 (the bad statement), reconstructing the table to its pre-incident state. After validation, the corrected data was loaded back into production. No data beyond the affected column values was lost because binlogs covered the entire gap.
prevention: Enable SET sql_safe_updates=1 in operator sessions (rejects UPDATE/DELETE without a key-based WHERE/LIMIT); run destructive statements only inside a transaction with a SELECT preview and explicit COMMIT; restrict direct prod write access and require change review for ad-hoc DML; verify backups + continuous binlog and rehearse PITR; consider a pt-osc/guardrail wrapper for manual edits.

title: Disk filling from unrotated binary logs and growing ibdata1
problem: Monitoring alerted that the database host's data volume was rapidly approaching full. Left unchecked, MySQL would have stopped accepting writes and crashed, threatening an outage.
symptoms: Steady, fast disk growth on /var/lib/mysql; dozens of large mysql-bin.* files accumulating; the shared ibdata1 file kept growing and never shrank; growth accelerated after a large data import.

102G   /var/lib/mysql/ibdata1

mysql> SHOW BINARY LOGS;

| Log_name         | File_size  |
+------------------+------------+
| mysql-bin.000180 | 1073741312 |
| ... (140 files) ...           |
| mysql-bin.000320 | 734881290  |
