mysql> SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_expire_logs_seconds';
+----------------------------+-------+
| Variable_name              | Value |
+----------------------------+-------+
| binlog_expire_logs_seconds | 0     |
+----------------------------+-------+
investigationSteps: Confirmed the volume was nearly full with df -h and then found what was consuming space using du -xh --max-depth=1 /var/lib/mysql | sort -h.
Identified two consumers: a large set of binary logs (SHOW BINARY LOGS revealed ~140 files) and a very large monolithic ibdata1.
Checked retention config: SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_expire_logs_seconds'; was 0 (no expiry), explaining the binlog pile-up.
Verified which binlogs were still needed by replicas before purging: on each replica ran SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G to note Source_Log_File so as not to delete logs still required for replication.

Checked innodb_file_per_table to understand why ibdata1 grew monolithically: SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_file_per_table'; found OFF, so all table/undo data lived in the shared, non-shrinking ibdata1 (made worse by the recent large import).
rootCause: Binary logs were never expiring (binlog_expire_logs_seconds=0) so they accumulated indefinitely, and innodb_file_per_table was OFF, so all data went into a single shared ibdata1 that grows but never shrinks — a large import inflated it permanently. Together they filled the disk.
resolution: Reclaimed binlog space safely: SET PERSIST binlog_expire_logs_seconds=604800; (7 days) and purged old logs not needed by replicas: PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE '2026-06-10 00:00:00'; freeing ~60GB immediately. For ibdata1 growth, enabled innodb_file_per_table=ON going forward and scheduled a rebuild (logical dump + reload into a fresh instance with file-per-table) to move tables into individually reclaimable .ibd files; truncated unused undo. Confirmed df dropped back to safe levels.
prevention: Set binlog_expire_logs_seconds (or expire_logs_days) with sane retention and rely on replica acknowledgment before purge; keep innodb_file_per_table=ON so space can be reclaimed per table; monitor and alert on disk usage at 80%; track ibdata1/binlog growth trends; size import jobs and run OPTIMIZE/rebuild after large data churn.

title: Sales report shows inflated totals from a one-to-many JOIN double-counting
problem: The daily revenue dashboard suddenly reported totals roughly 2-3x higher than finance's reconciled figures. The wrong numbers were being used in an executive report, risking bad business decisions.
symptoms: Reported revenue far exceeded the sum of payments; order counts looked inflated; the discrepancy grew with orders that had multiple line items or multiple shipments; the underlying tables were correct when queried individually.
logs:
-- Reported (buggy) query
SELECT o.order_id, SUM(o.total_cents) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.order_id;

-- Sanity check that exposed the inflation
mysql> SELECT o.order_id, o.total_cents, COUNT(oi.id) AS item_rows,
    ->        o.total_cents * COUNT(oi.id) AS counted_as
    -> FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id=o.order_id
    -> WHERE o.order_id=88120 GROUP BY o.order_id, o.total_cents;
+----------+-------------+-----------+------------+
| order_id | total_cents | item_rows | counted_as |
+----------+-------------+-----------+------------+
|    88120 |        4500 |         3 |      13500 |  <-- counted 3x
+----------+-------------+-----------+------------+

mysql> SELECT SUM(total_cents) FROM orders;            -- 9,841,200 (true)
mysql> SELECT SUM(o.total_cents) FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id=o.order_id;  -- 24,118,900 (inflated)
investigationSteps: Reproduced the gap by comparing the report total to a ground-truth aggregate: SELECT SUM(total_cents) FROM orders; versus the joined sum, confirming the joined version was inflated.
Isolated a single order (order_id=88120) and ran the join with COUNT(oi.id) to see the order header row fanned out once per line item — proving the order total was summed multiple times.

Reviewed a recent report change in version control and found a JOIN to order_items had been added (for a new 'items per order' column) without adjusting the revenue aggregation, turning a 1:1 sum into a 1:many sum.

Checked for a related anti-pattern: confirmed whether any LEFT JOINs had a WHERE filter on the right table that silently turned them into INNER JOINs (it did on a returns join, dropping orders with no return).
Validated candidate fixes (pre-aggregate the child table, or use COUNT(DISTINCT)) against the known-good orders total before shipping.
rootCause: The report joined orders to the one-to-many order_items table and then summed orders.total_cents. The join duplicated each order header row once per line item, so SUM(total_cents) counted each order's total as many times as it had items — classic fan-out double counting. (A secondary bug: a LEFT JOIN to returns with a WHERE condition on the returns table had collapsed it into an INNER JOIN, dropping non-returned orders.)
resolution: Removed the fan-out by aggregating revenue from the order grain and joining a pre-aggregated child set: SELECT o.order_id, o.total_cents AS revenue, COALESCE(i.item_count,0) AS items FROM orders o LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) item_count FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) i ON i.order_id=o.order_id; For dashboard totals used SUM over the de-duplicated order grain (or SUM(DISTINCT) on the header). Fixed the LEFT JOIN by moving the returns predicate into the ON clause. Re-ran the report and it matched finance's reconciled total exactly.
prevention: Define the reporting grain explicitly and pre-aggregate child tables before joining (or use COUNT/SUM DISTINCT carefully); add reconciliation tests that compare report totals against independent ground-truth aggregates; put filter conditions for outer-joined tables in the ON clause, not WHERE; peer-review SQL changes to reports and snapshot expected totals in CI.

title: MongoDB primary stepped down during failover, causing transient write errors
problem: The application experienced a burst of write failures for several seconds. MongoDB writes threw 'not primary' / 'node is not in primary or recovering state', and a few user actions errored out before service self-recovered.
symptoms: Errors clustered in a ~10-15s window; reads (from secondaries) were mostly fine but writes failed; the cluster briefly had no primary then elected a new one; the old primary had a heartbeat hiccup just before the election.
investigationSteps: Confirmed it was a failover, not a full outage, by running rs.status() and seeing a new PRIMARY (mongo-b) with a fresh election term and recent electionDate.
Read the mongod logs on the old primary (REPL/ELECTION components) and saw it stepped down after missing heartbeats, triggering an election that completed in ~2-3s.
Checked the heartbeat/network cause: reviewed rs.status() members[].lastHeartbeat and host metrics; found a brief network blip / CPU spike on the old primary that delayed heartbeats past the timeout.

Examined the application's MongoClient settings and write concern; found short/disabled retryWrites and a low server-selection/socket timeout, so transient 'not primary' errors surfaced to users instead of being retried after the new primary was elected.
Verified data integrity post-failover: confirmed acknowledged writes used majority write concern and no acknowledged data was lost during the term change.
rootCause: A transient heartbeat/network disruption on the primary caused it to step down and the replica set to hold an election. During the brief no-primary window, write commands returned 'not primary' (NotWritablePrimary). Because the application was not configured for retryable writes (and had aggressive timeouts), these normally-transient errors were exposed to end users.
resolution: Made writes resilient to elections: enabled retryWrites=true in the connection string and set an appropriate serverSelectionTimeoutMS (e.g., 30s) so the driver waits out and retries on the new primary. Standardized on majority write concern for durability across failovers. Addressed the trigger by stabilizing the primary's network/host (resource limits and heartbeat settings reviewed). After the changes, simulating a stepdown (rs.stepDown()) produced no user-visible write errors — the driver transparently retried.
prevention: Always run with retryable writes and sensible server-selection timeouts so app survives elections; use w:'majority' write concern; ensure odd member count with a healthy voting majority; monitor replica-set elections and heartbeat latency; provision the primary with headroom and stable networking; periodically game-day test failover with rs.stepDown().

title: MongoDB query slow from a full collection scan (no index)
problem: A product search/filter API on MongoDB became slow as the collection grew. Response times for filtered queries climbed to several seconds, degrading the catalog browsing experience.
symptoms: Latency scaled with collection size; CPU on the mongod node rose during query bursts; queries filtering on a non-_id field were the slow ones; explain() showed the engine examining the entire collection.
investigationSteps: Reproduced the slow query and ran db.products.find({...}).explain("executionStats") — saw stage COLLSCAN, totalKeysExamined=0, and docsExamined equal to the whole collection (~1.98M).
Enabled the database profiler / slow-query log: db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 100 }); and confirmed the same COLLSCAN planSummary appearing for category/active filters.
Listed existing indexes with db.products.getIndexes() and found only the default _id index — nothing supporting the category/active predicate.
Estimated selectivity with db.products.aggregate([{ $group: { _id: '$category', n: { $sum: 1 } } }]) to choose effective leading fields for a compound index.
Created a compound index and re-ran explain() to confirm the planner switched from COLLSCAN to an IXSCAN before rolling to production.
rootCause: The products collection had no index covering the query predicate (category, active), so MongoDB performed a full collection scan (COLLSCAN), examining every document. As the collection grew toward ~2M documents, scan time grew proportionally and queries slowed to seconds.
resolution: Created a compound index matching the equality filter: db.products.createIndex({ category: 1, active: 1 }); (built in the background to avoid blocking). After indexing, explain("executionStats") showed stage IXSCAN with totalKeysExamined ≈ nReturned, docsExamined dropped from ~1.98M to ~42, and executionTimeMillis fell from ~3120ms to single-digit ms.
prevention: Index fields used in frequent query predicates and sorts (follow the ESR — Equality, Sort, Range — order for compound indexes); keep the profiler on with a slowms threshold and alert on COLLSCAN planSummary; review explain() for new queries in code review; periodically audit getIndexes() vs actual query patterns.

title: HTTPS site shows certificate errors for all users
problem: Every visitor to https://shop.example.com sees a browser security warning and cannot proceed. The site is effectively down for all customers across all browsers and devices.
symptoms: Chrome shows NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID; Firefox shows SEC_ERROR_EXPIRED_CERTIFICATE; mobile apps report 'certificate has expired'. The padlock is red. The issue is global and not user-specific.
logs:
$ curl -vI https://shop.example.com
*   Trying 203.0.113.10:443...
* Connected to shop.example.com (203.0.113.10) port 443
* ALPN: offers h2,http/1.1
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
* Server certificate:
*  subject: CN=shop.example.com
*  start date: Mar 14 00:00:00 2025 GMT
*  expire date: Jun 12 23:59:59 2026 GMT
* SSL certificate problem: certificate has expired
* Closing connection
curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: certificate has expired

$ echo | openssl s_client -connect shop.example.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
notBefore=Mar 14 00:00:00 2025 GMT
notAfter=Jun 12 23:59:59 2026 GMT
investigationSteps: Reproduce the error in an incognito browser and with curl -vI to confirm it is not a local/client cache issue and affects everyone.
Run openssl s_client -connect shop.example.com:443 -servername shop.example.com to retrieve the live certificate presented by the server.
Pipe the output to openssl x509 -noout -dates and compare notAfter against the current date (date -u).
Confirm notAfter (Jun 12 2026) is earlier than today (Jun 17 2026), proving the certificate expired 5 days ago.
Check the ACME/Let's Encrypt renewal: review certbot logs (/var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log) and run certbot certificates to see expiry and renewal status.
Identify that the automated renewal cron/timer failed silently and the renewed cert was never deployed.
rootCause: The TLS certificate's validity period ended (expired). The automated renewal job had been failing for weeks (its systemd timer was disabled during an unrelated patch), so no one noticed until the old certificate lapsed.
resolution: Renewed the certificate immediately with 'certbot renew --force-renewal', reloaded nginx ('nginx -s reload') so it served the new cert, and verified with openssl s_client that the new notAfter date was ~90 days out.
prevention: Re-enable and monitor the certbot systemd timer; add external certificate-expiry monitoring (e.g. a check that alerts at 30/14/7 days remaining) and a synthetic HTTPS probe so an expired or soon-to-expire cert pages the on-call engineer well before it impacts users.

title: After migration the site works by IP but not by hostname
problem: Following a server migration to a new host, the application is reachable when browsing directly to the new IP, but the public hostname www.example.com still loads the old (now decommissioned) server or fails entirely.
symptoms: Browsing http://203.0.113.50 shows the new site correctly. Browsing http://www.example.com shows a connection refused/timeout or the old maintenance page. Some users see the new site, others see the old one (split-brain depending on cached DNS).
logs:
$ dig +short www.example.com A
198.51.100.20

$ dig www.example.com A +noall +answer
www.example.com.   3600   IN   A   198.51.100.20

# New server is actually at 203.0.113.50; DNS still points to the OLD IP 198.51.100.20
$ curl -sI http://203.0.113.50 | head -n1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
$ curl -sI http://www.example.com | head -n1
curl: (7) Failed to connect to www.example.com port 80: Connection refused

$ dig www.example.com A @8.8.8.8 +short
198.51.100.20
investigationSteps: Confirm the new server answers directly: curl -sI http://203.0.113.50 returns 200, so the app and web server are healthy.
Resolve the hostname with dig +short www.example.com A and observe it returns the OLD IP 198.51.100.20, not the new 203.0.113.50.
Query an authoritative/public resolver (dig www.example.com @8.8.8.8) to distinguish a stale local cache from an actual wrong record at the authoritative zone.
Inspect the record's TTL with dig www.example.com A +noall +answer; note TTL=3600 (1 hour), explaining slow propagation if it was just changed.
Log into the DNS provider and verify the A record value — find it was never updated (or was updated but cached clients still hold the old answer until TTL expires).
Confirm the old IP is being decommissioned, which is why some clients now get connection refused.
rootCause: The DNS A record for www.example.com was not updated (or was updated late) to the new server's IP. Because the record had a 1-hour TTL that was not lowered before the migration, resolvers and clients continued returning the old IP for up to an hour, sending users to the retired server.
resolution: Updated the A record at the authoritative DNS provider to 203.0.113.50, and as a stopgap kept the old server online (proxying to the new one) until propagation completed. Verified with dig against multiple public resolvers that the new IP was being returned everywhere.
prevention: Plan DNS cutovers in advance: lower the record TTL (e.g. to 60s) 24-48 hours before migration so changes propagate quickly, update the record as part of the migration runbook, and keep the old endpoint serving/redirecting until all caches expire. Add a post-migration check that dig returns the expected IP.

title: 502 Bad Gateway for all users immediately after deploy
problem: Right after a code deploy, every request to the site returns 502 Bad Gateway. The nginx reverse proxy is up, but it cannot reach the application backend, so the entire site is down.
symptoms: Users see the default nginx '502 Bad Gateway' page. All endpoints fail uniformly. The outage began at the exact timestamp of the deploy.
logs:
# nginx error.log
2026/06/17 09:14:02 [error] 1123#1123: *5567 connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream, client: 198.51.100.7, server: app.example.com, request: "GET / HTTP/1.1", upstream: "http://127.0.0.1:8080/", host: "app.example.com"

$ curl -sI http://app.example.com/ | head -n1
HTTP/1.1 502 Bad Gateway

$ ss -lntp | grep 8080
(no output — nothing is listening on 8080)

$ systemctl status app.service
  app.service - Application Server
     Active: failed (Result: exit-code) since Wed 2026-06-17 09:13:58 UTC
   Main PID: 4471 (code=exited, status=1/FAILURE)
investigationSteps: Confirm the proxy itself is alive (systemctl status nginx = active) and that the 502 is generated by nginx, not the app.
Read nginx error.log and find 'connect() failed (111: Connection refused) ... upstream: http://127.0.0.1:8080' — nginx cannot reach the backend port.
Check whether anything is listening on the backend port with ss -lntp | grep 8080; find nothing is bound.
Inspect the application service state with systemctl status app.service and find it is 'failed' with exit status 1, starting at the deploy time.
Read the application's own log/journalctl -u app.service to find the crash reason (e.g. a bad config value or missing env var introduced by the deploy).
Correlate the failure timestamp (09:13:58) with the deploy to confirm the new release crashed on startup.
rootCause: The newly deployed application build crashed on startup (a syntax/config error introduced in the release), so the backend process exited and nothing was listening on port 8080. nginx, still running, returned 502 because the upstream connection was refused.
resolution: Rolled back to the previous known-good release and restarted the service ('systemctl restart app.service'); confirmed it was listening with ss -lntp on 8080 and that curl returned 200. The faulty config error was then fixed and re-deployed safely.
prevention: Gate deploys behind a readiness/health check that the orchestrator must see green before shifting traffic; use rolling or blue-green deploys so a crashed new version never takes down the old one; and add a startup smoke test in CI so config errors are caught before reaching production.

title: Intermittent 504 Gateway Timeout under load
problem: Users intermittently get 504 Gateway Timeout, especially on report-generation and search pages. The frequency increases during peak hours. Lighter pages still work.
symptoms: Roughly 1 in 10 requests to /reports and /search return a '504 Gateway Timeout' after a long hang (~60s). Static pages and the homepage are unaffected. Errors cluster during business-hours load.
logs:
# nginx error.log
2026/06/17 14:22:51 [error] 2210#2210: *88231 upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while reading response header from upstream, client: 203.0.113.40, server: app.example.com, request: "GET /reports?range=90d HTTP/1.1", upstream: "http://10.0.2.15:8080/reports?range=90d", host: "app.example.com"

# nginx access.log (note request_time)
203.0.113.40 - - [17/Jun/2026:14:22:51] "GET /reports?range=90d HTTP/1.1" 504 167 rt=60.001 uct=0.001 uht=- urt=60.000

# nginx config
proxy_read_timeout 60s;

# backend slow query log
2026-06-17 14:22:00 [SLOW] SELECT ... FROM events WHERE ts > ... GROUP BY ... duration=72143ms rows_examined=18402551
investigationSteps: Confirm the status code and timing: nginx access.log shows 504 with rt=60.001 and urt=60.000, meaning the upstream hit nginx's read timeout exactly.
Read nginx error.log to see 'upstream timed out (110) while reading response header from upstream' for the slow endpoints.
Verify the configured proxy_read_timeout (60s) and note the request took longer than that, so nginx aborted while the backend was still working.
Reproduce against the backend directly (curl -w '%{time_total}' http://10.0.2.15:8080/reports?range=90d) and observe it takes ~72s — slower than the proxy timeout.
Check backend resource/DB metrics and the slow-query log; find a heavy aggregation query scanning ~18M rows without a supporting index.
Conclude the backend is genuinely slow (not down), so the fix is to speed up the backend and/or align timeouts, not to restart the proxy.
rootCause: A backend report query was unoptimized (full scan over millions of rows), so under load it routinely took ~70s — longer than nginx's 60s proxy_read_timeout. nginx terminated the connection and returned 504 even though the backend would eventually have answered.
resolution: Added a covering index on the events(ts) column and introduced query result caching, cutting the report query to <2s. As an immediate mitigation, the proxy_read_timeout was temporarily raised and a 'report is generating' async pattern was added so requests no longer block.
prevention: Monitor upstream response time (urt) and alert on p95 latency creeping toward the proxy timeout; add slow-query alerting and index reviews; offload long-running work to background jobs; and document sane, consistent timeout values across the proxy and backend.

title: Service port unreachable from some networks (timeout vs refused)
problem: A newly exposed API on port 8443 is reachable from the office network but times out from the public internet and from the partner's network. The service is running and the local firewall looks open.
symptoms: From the office: connection succeeds. From external networks: 'curl: (28) Connection timed out' on port 8443; the connection just hangs with no RST. SSH on 22 and HTTPS on 443 still work from everywhere.
logs:
# From an external host
$ nc -zv api.example.com 8443
nc: connect to api.example.com port 8443 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress

$ curl -v https://api.example.com:8443/health
*   Trying 203.0.113.10:8443...
* connect to 203.0.113.10 port 8443 failed: Connection timed out
* Failed to connect to api.example.com port 8443 after 129642 ms: Connection timed out
curl: (28) Failed to connect to api.example.com port 8443

# On the server itself — service IS listening and locally reachable
$ ss -lntp | grep 8443
LISTEN 0  4096  0.0.0.0:8443  0.0.0.0:*  users:(("api",pid=991,fd=7))
$ curl -sI https://127.0.0.1:8443/health -k | head -n1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
investigationSteps: Resolve the hostname (dig +short api.example.com) to rule out DNS and confirm everyone targets the same IP 203.0.113.10.
On the server confirm the service is bound to 0.0.0.0:8443 (not 127.0.0.1) using ss -lntp, and that curl to localhost:8443 returns 200 — so the app is healthy.
From an external host test raw TCP with nc -zv api.example.com 8443 and observe a TIMEOUT (not 'refused').

Interpret the signal: a TIMEOUT (silent drop, no RST) points to a packet-filtering firewall/security group dropping the SYN, whereas 'Connection refused' would mean the host got the packet but nothing was listening.
Compare with working ports (nc -zv api.example.com 443 succeeds), confirming the host is reachable and only 8443 is being filtered.
Review the cloud security group / network ACL and host firewall rules for port 8443 and find no inbound allow rule for 0.0.0.0/0 (only the office CIDR was whitelisted).
rootCause: A firewall / cloud security-group rule did not permit inbound traffic to TCP 8443 from the internet — only the office subnet had been whitelisted. External SYN packets were silently dropped, which manifests as a connection timeout (rather than 'refused', which a closed-but-reachable port would give).
resolution: Added an inbound security-group rule allowing TCP 8443 from the required source ranges (and tightened it to the partner CIDR rather than 0.0.0.0/0 for safety). Re-tested with nc -zv and curl from external networks and confirmed immediate connectivity.
prevention: Treat 'timeout vs refused' as a first-class diagnostic: timeout = filtered, refused = nothing listening. Manage firewall/security-group rules as code with reviews, document required ingress ports for each service, and add an external reachability probe so a missing rule is caught at deploy time.

title: Load balancer returns 503 with all backends unhealthy
problem: The load balancer is returning 503 Service Unavailable for every request and reports that all backend targets are 'unhealthy', even though the application processes appear to be running on every node.
symptoms: Users see a 503 error page served by the load balancer. The LB target/health dashboard shows 0 healthy / N unhealthy targets. The app process is up on each node and answers on its app port locally.
logs:
# LB health check is configured for GET /healthz on port 8080
# On a backend node — app answers / but NOT /healthz
$ curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8080/ | head -n1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
$ curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz | head -n1
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

# LB access log
10.0.0.5 - - [17/Jun/2026:11:02:14] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 503 190 "-" "-" TargetGroup: app-tg health: 0/4 healthy

# Target health detail
Target 10.0.2.11:8080  State: unhealthy  Reason: Health checks failed with these codes: [404]
Target 10.0.2.12:8080  State: unhealthy  Reason: Health checks failed with these codes: [404]
investigationSteps: Confirm the 503 is generated by the load balancer (its access log shows 503 with 'health: 0/4 healthy'), not by the backends.
Read the target-health detail and note the failure reason: 'Health checks failed with codes: [404]'.
Inspect the configured health-check path/port on the LB target group (GET /healthz on 8080).
On a backend node, curl both the real path and the health path: curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8080/ returns 200 but http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz returns 404.
Conclude the application is actually serving traffic fine but no longer exposes the /healthz endpoint the LB probes, so the LB marks every target down and refuses to route.
Check the recent change history and find the health endpoint was renamed (or removed) in a recent release without updating the LB configuration.
rootCause: A recent release removed/renamed the /healthz endpoint the load balancer health check targeted. The probe began receiving HTTP 404, so the LB marked all targets unhealthy and stopped forwarding traffic, returning 503 — even though the app itself was healthy.
resolution: Restored the /healthz endpoint in the application (a lightweight handler returning 200) and redeployed; as an immediate fix the LB health-check path was pointed at an existing 200-returning route. Within one health-check interval all targets returned to healthy and the 503s cleared.
prevention: Treat the health-check contract as protected: cover /healthz with an integration test, document it, and review LB/app changes together. Configure health checks to require a 200 and alert when healthy-target count drops, so a broken probe pages before it takes the whole pool offline.

title: Intermittent failures for about 25% of users
problem: About a quarter of requests fail or are slow, seemingly at random. Retrying often succeeds. The pattern is consistent with one bad member of a four-node backend pool (or one degraded availability zone).
symptoms: Roughly 25% of page loads return 500/connection-reset or take very long; refreshing usually fixes it. No single user is fully blocked; failures are spread evenly. Error rate is steady at ~25%, not spiking.
logs:
# nginx upstream block has 4 backends (round-robin)
upstream app { server 10.0.2.11:8080; server 10.0.2.12:8080; server 10.0.2.13:8080; server 10.0.2.14:8080; }

# Tail of nginx error.log — failures only ever name ONE upstream
2026/06/17 16:05:11 [error] *90021 upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream, upstream: "http://10.0.2.13:8080/api/orders"
2026/06/17 16:05:13 [error] *90044 connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream, upstream: "http://10.0.2.13:8080/"

# Probe each node directly
$ for ip in 11 12 13 14; do echo -n "10.0.2.$ip: "; curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" http://10.0.2.$ip:8080/healthz; done
10.0.2.11: 200 0.04s
10.0.2.12: 200 0.05s
10.0.2.13: 000 10.001s
10.0.2.14: 200 0.04s
investigationSteps: Quantify the failure rate from the LB/nginx access logs and confirm it is steady (~25%), pointing to 1 of 4 equally-weighted backends rather than a global fault.
Grep nginx error.log for the upstream field and notice every error names the same node, 10.0.2.13.
Probe each backend individually with a curl loop hitting /healthz and compare status/latency; find 10.0.2.13 returns 000 after a 10s timeout while the other three return 200 quickly.

On the bad node, inspect the service (systemctl status, journalctl) and resource usage (top, df -h, dmesg) to see why it is degraded — e.g. the app is hung, the disk is full, or it is in a failing AZ.
Confirm round-robin is sending ~1/4 of traffic to the dead node with no passive failover configured (max_fails/fail_timeout not set), explaining the intermittent ~25% errors.
Validate the hypothesis by temporarily removing 10.0.2.13 from rotation and watching the error rate drop to ~0%.
rootCause: One backend node (10.0.2.13) was degraded — its app process was hung/unresponsive (and the node sat in an impaired AZ). Because the load balancer used plain round-robin with no health-based ejection, ~25% of requests were still routed to the dead node and failed, while retries that landed on a healthy node succeeded.
resolution: Drained and removed the unhealthy node from the pool, then rebuilt/replaced the instance. Re-added it only after /healthz returned 200. Error rate dropped to near zero immediately after ejection.
prevention: Enable active and passive health checks on the LB/proxy (e.g. nginx max_fails/fail_timeout or LB target health) so a bad node is automatically ejected; spread nodes across multiple AZs with health-aware routing; and alert on per-node error-rate divergence so one sick member is caught before users notice.

title: Site loads in browsers but curl/API clients fail TLS (incomplete chain)
problem: The website opens fine in major desktop browsers, but curl, mobile apps, and server-to-server API clients fail the TLS handshake with a verification error. The leaf certificate is valid; the server is not sending the intermediate CA certificate.
symptoms: Browsers show a valid padlock. curl reports 'unable to get local issuer certificate'; Java clients throw PKIX path building failed; some Android devices fail while others (with cached intermediates) succeed — making it look intermittent.
logs:
$ curl -vI https://api.example.com
*   Trying 203.0.113.10:443...
* Server certificate:
*  subject: CN=api.example.com
*  issuer: CN=R3, O=Let's Encrypt
* SSL certificate verify result: unable to get local issuer certificate (20)
curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate

$ echo | openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com 2>/dev/null | grep -E "Certificate chain|s:|i:"
Certificate chain
 0 s:CN=api.example.com
   i:C=US, O=Let's Encrypt, CN=R3
# <-- only ONE certificate sent; the intermediate (R3) and root are missing

$ openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -verify_return_error </dev/null
Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)
investigationSteps: Reproduce the split behavior: site loads in a browser but curl -vI returns 'unable to get local issuer certificate (20)'.
Dump the presented chain with openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com and count the certificates returned.
Observe only certificate '0' (the leaf) is sent — there is no intermediate '1' — and the verify return code is 21 'unable to verify the first certificate'.

Explain the browser-vs-client discrepancy: browsers often cache or fetch intermediates via AIA, so they paper over the gap, while strict clients (curl, Java) require the server to send the full chain.
Inspect the server's certificate file referenced by ssl_certificate in nginx and confirm it contains only the leaf, not the leaf+intermediate (fullchain) bundle.
Verify the fix target: the server must present leaf + intermediate so any client can build a path to a trusted root.
rootCause: The web server was configured with only the leaf certificate (cert.pem) instead of the full chain (fullchain.pem that includes the intermediate CA). Clients that don't fetch intermediates themselves could not build a trust path, causing TLS verification failures, while lenient browsers still succeeded.
resolution: Updated nginx's ssl_certificate to point at fullchain.pem (leaf + intermediate) and reloaded the service. Re-ran openssl s_client and confirmed both certificate 0 (leaf) and certificate 1 (R3 intermediate) were now presented, and curl returned 200 with verify result OK.
prevention: Always deploy the full chain (fullchain.pem), not the bare leaf. Validate the served chain after every cert deployment with openssl s_client or an external SSL checker, and test with a strict client (curl --cert-status / no system-cached intermediates) so chain gaps are caught before clients break.

title: Site-wide DNS resolution failure (resolver unreachable / bad resolv.conf)
problem: A server suddenly cannot resolve any hostname. Outbound API calls, package installs, and dependent services all fail, even though the network link is up and the server can reach IPs directly.
symptoms: Applications log 'Name or service not known' / 'Temporary failure in name resolution'. ping by hostname fails but ping by IP succeeds. curl to any domain fails at the resolution step; curl to a raw IP works.
logs:
$ curl -v https://api.partner.com
* Could not resolve host: api.partner.com
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: api.partner.com

$ ping -c1 api.partner.com
ping: api.partner.com: Name or service not known
$ ping -c1 1.1.1.1
64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=57 time=4.21 ms   # raw IP works

$ dig example.com
;; communications error to 10.0.0.2#53: connection timed out
;; no servers could be reached

$ cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.0.0.2   # this resolver is decommissioned / unreachable

$ dig @1.1.1.1 example.com +short
93.184.216.34          # resolution works against a reachable resolver
investigationSteps: Confirm the failure is name resolution, not connectivity: ping/curl by hostname fails ('Could not resolve host') but ping to a raw IP (1.1.1.1) succeeds.
Run dig example.com and observe ';; no servers could be reached' / 'communications error to 10.0.0.2#53', identifying the configured resolver.
Inspect /etc/resolv.conf and find it lists only nameserver 10.0.0.2.
Test that resolver explicitly with dig @10.0.0.2 example.com — it times out, proving the DNS server is unreachable/decommissioned.
Cross-check with a known-good resolver: dig @1.1.1.1 example.com returns an answer, confirming DNS itself works and only the configured resolver is the problem.
Determine why resolv.conf is wrong (e.g. it was overwritten by DHCP/cloud-init or the internal resolver was retired).
rootCause: The only nameserver listed in /etc/resolv.conf (10.0.0.2) had been decommissioned, so every DNS query timed out with no fallback. The link and routing were fine; the host simply had no working resolver, breaking all hostname-based connections.
resolution: Pointed /etc/resolv.conf at reachable resolvers (the new internal resolver plus a public fallback such as 1.1.1.1) and restarted the resolver service. Verified with dig and curl that hostnames resolved again, restoring dependent services.
prevention: Configure at least two reachable nameservers for redundancy, manage resolv.conf via the systemd-resolved/DHCP source of truth so it isn't silently overwritten, and add monitoring that periodically resolves a canary hostname so resolver outages are detected immediately.

title: Some requests hit the wrong app (reverse-proxy routing misconfiguration)
problem: After adding a new microservice behind the shared reverse proxy, certain paths intermittently return responses from the wrong application — e.g. /api/orders sometimes returns the inventory service's output. Routing is non-deterministic.
symptoms: Calls to /api/orders occasionally return JSON shaped like the inventory service, or 404s from a service that shouldn't own that path. Users report 'wrong data' and mismatched responses; the same request works on retry. No TLS or connectivity errors.
logs:
# nginx config — two location blocks overlap / order matters
server {
  listen 443 ssl;
  server_name app.example.com;
  location /api/ { proxy_pass http://inventory_svc; }      # too-broad prefix
  location /api/orders { proxy_pass http://orders_svc; }   # more specific but shadowed by regex elsewhere
  location ~ ^/api/ { proxy_pass http://inventory_svc; }   # regex match wins over prefix in nginx
}

# nginx access.log — same path, different upstream
203.0.113.9 - - [17/Jun/2026:13:40:01] "GET /api/orders/123 HTTP/1.1" 200 512 upstream: 10.0.3.20:8080 (inventory_svc)
203.0.113.9 - - [17/Jun/2026:13:40:55] "GET /api/orders/123 HTTP/1.1" 200 488 upstream: 10.0.3.30:8080 (orders_svc)

$ curl -s http://10.0.3.30:8080/api/orders/123 | head -c 60
{"order_id":123,"status":"shipped"}   # orders_svc = correct
$ curl -s http://10.0.3.20:8080/api/orders/123 | head -c 60
{"sku":"123","warehouse":"A"}        # inventory_svc = wrong app
investigationSteps: Reproduce by hitting /api/orders/123 repeatedly and capturing the 'upstream' field in nginx access.log; observe the same path resolving to two different upstreams (inventory_svc vs orders_svc).
Query each backend directly with curl to confirm which app owns the path: 10.0.3.30 returns the correct order JSON, 10.0.3.20 returns inventory data.
Review the nginx server block and list all location directives matching /api/orders, noting overlapping prefix and regex locations.

Apply nginx's matching precedence rules (exact > longest prefix with '^~' > first matching regex > longest prefix) and find the regex 'location ~ ^/api/' is winning over the intended 'location /api/orders' prefix.

Confirm the misroute is deterministic per matching rule (the apparent randomness came from config reloads / multiple upstreams in a group), and that the broad regex was added recently for the new service.
Validate the corrected matching by testing the new config with nginx -t before reload.
rootCause: Overlapping nginx location blocks with a too-broad regex ('location ~ ^/api/' -> inventory_svc) shadowed the intended specific route ('location /api/orders' -> orders_svc). Because nginx evaluates regex locations before plain prefixes, order requests were proxied to the inventory service.
resolution: Rewrote the routing so the specific path used a higher-priority match (e.g. 'location ^~ /api/orders { proxy_pass http://orders_svc; }') and scoped the regex narrowly so it no longer captured /api/orders. Tested with nginx -t, reloaded, and confirmed /api/orders consistently hit orders_svc in the access log.
prevention: Define explicit, non-overlapping routing rules and understand the proxy's match-precedence order; review proxy config changes when onboarding new services; and add contract tests / synthetic checks that assert each path reaches its intended upstream so misroutes are caught in CI rather than by users.

title: Users locked out: SSO login fails after token-signing certificate expired
problem: Starting at 08:00, no users could log into the customer portal. The login page redirected to the corporate Identity Provider (IdP) and returned to the app with an authentication error. All new and existing sessions were affected once tokens needed re-validation.
symptoms: Every login attempt ends on an error page reading 'Authentication failed'. Users who were already logged in get kicked out within minutes. Support phones light up across all regions simultaneously. Health check on the app itself is green; only the auth flow is broken.
logs:
2026-06-17T08:01:14Z [auth-gateway] WARN  SAML response received from IdP, validating signature
2026-06-17T08:01:14Z [auth-gateway] ERROR Signature validation failed: signing certificate is expired
2026-06-17T08:01:14Z [auth-gateway] ERROR   notAfter=2026-06-17T00:00:00Z now=2026-06-17T08:01:14Z thumbprint=A1:F3:9C:...:7E
2026-06-17T08:01:14Z [auth-gateway] ERROR org.opensaml.xmlsec.signature.support.SignatureException: Validation of signature failed

investigationSteps: Confirmed scope and impact: reproduced the failure with a test account; verified all regions and all user types are affected, so it is not user-specific or region-specific.
Checked the app's own health endpoint and database — both healthy, ruling out an app-tier or DB outage.
Read the auth-gateway logs and found the SAML signature validation error pointing at an expired signing certificate (notAfter earlier today).
Checked the IdP federation metadata and the certificate thumbprint configured in the gateway; confirmed the token-signing cert expired at 2026-06-17T00:00:00Z.
Correlated with the change calendar: the IdP team had rotated the signing cert overnight but the new public cert was never published/imported into the app's trust store.

resolution: Imported the new signing certificate and refreshed the IdP federation metadata into the auth-gateway trust store, then reloaded the gateway configuration. Logins recovered immediately; users re-authenticated normally.
prevention: Automate certificate expiry monitoring with alerts at 30/14/7 days before notAfter for all federation certs. Subscribe the relying party to the IdP metadata URL so cert rotations are picked up automatically, and add SSO certs to a shared renewal runbook owned jointly by the IdP and app teams.

title: API endpoint times out when a downstream pricing service is slow
problem: The /v1/checkout/quote endpoint began returning 504 Gateway Timeout intermittently, then almost continuously. The endpoint synchronously calls an internal pricing service that had become slow, and the caller's threads were exhausted waiting on it.
symptoms: Customers see a spinning checkout that eventually errors. p99 latency on /quote jumps from ~200ms to 30s. The API gateway logs a rising count of 504s. Other endpoints in the same service also slow down as the request thread pool saturates.
logs:
2026-06-17T11:42:07Z [api] INFO  GET /v1/checkout/quote orderId=88231 -> calling pricing-svc
2026-06-17T11:42:37Z [api] ERROR Upstream call timed out after 30000ms target=http://pricing-svc/internal/price
2026-06-17T11:42:37Z [api] ERROR java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException: Did not observe any item or terminal signal within 30000ms
2026-06-17T11:42:37Z [gateway] 504 GET /v1/checkout/quote rt=30012ms
2026-06-17T11:42:40Z [api] WARN  HikariPool / web thread pool exhausted: active=200 idle=0 waiting=145
2026-06-17T11:43:00Z [pricing-svc] WARN  slow query: SELECT * FROM rate_card WHERE region=? took 28774ms
investigationSteps: Identified the failing endpoint and confirmed it returns 504 from the gateway, indicating the backend did not respond in time rather than returning an error.
Traced a sample request and saw the api service blocking on an outbound call to pricing-svc for the full 30s timeout.
Checked pricing-svc health and metrics: CPU normal but request latency extremely high; logs showed a slow rate_card query taking ~28s.
Verified the api service thread pool was saturated (active=200, waiting=145), explaining why unrelated endpoints also slowed — the slow dependency was consuming all request threads.
Looked at the pricing-svc database and found a missing/at-capacity index after a recent data load, causing full table scans on rate_card.
Confirmed the api service had no circuit breaker or short timeout/fallback for this dependency, so slowness propagated upstream as full outages.
rootCause: A slow query in the downstream pricing service (full table scan on rate_card after a data load invalidated/lacked the index) caused 28s+ responses; the calling API had a long synchronous timeout and no circuit breaker, so its thread pool exhausted and the endpoint returned 504s.
resolution: Rebuilt the missing index on rate_card, which dropped pricing-svc latency back to ~40ms and cleared the 504s. As an immediate mitigation, the api timeout to pricing-svc was reduced and a circuit breaker with a cached-price fallback was enabled.
prevention: Add circuit breakers, bulkheads, and aggressive timeouts on all synchronous downstream calls. Alert on p99 latency and thread-pool saturation per service. Add slow-query monitoring and an index/health check to the data-load job so missing indexes are caught before traffic hits them.

title: RabbitMQ queue depth climbing because the consumer scaled to zero
problem: The order-processing queue depth climbed from near zero to over 50,000 messages within an hour and kept rising. Orders were accepted by the API and published successfully, but nothing downstream was processing them.
symptoms: Orders appear 'received' to customers but never progress to 'confirmed'. The RabbitMQ management UI shows messages.ready growing steadily with 0 consumers on the queue. No errors in the producing service. Fulfilment dashboard shows zero throughput.
logs:
2026-06-17T13:05:00Z [rabbitmq] queue=orders.process messages_ready=51230 messages_unacked=0 consumers=0
2026-06-17T13:05:00Z [rabbitmq] queue=orders.process publish_rate=42/s deliver_rate=0/s
2026-06-17T12:10:11Z [order-consumer] INFO  Received SIGTERM, shutting down gracefully
2026-06-17T12:10:12Z [order-consumer] INFO  Cancelled consumer tag amq.ctag-9f2 on queue orders.process
2026-06-17T12:10:13Z [k8s] order-consumer scaled replicas 3 -> 0 (HPA min replicas misconfigured to 0)
2026-06-17T13:04:55Z [k8s] order-consumer desired=0 available=0
investigationSteps: Opened the RabbitMQ management UI and confirmed messages_ready is rising while deliver_rate is 0 and consumers=0 — a classic 'nobody is consuming' pattern.
Confirmed the producer is healthy: publish_rate is normal and there are no publish errors, so messages are being enqueued correctly.
Checked the consumer deployment and found 0 running replicas of order-consumer.
Reviewed the orchestrator events and saw the consumer was scaled from 3 to 0 replicas; the HPA minReplicas had been changed to 0 in a recent config edit.
Read the consumer logs and saw a clean SIGTERM/graceful-shutdown at 12:10 with no crash, matching the scale-down rather than a failure.
Verified the queue had no consumer because the deployment intentionally (but wrongly) sat at zero replicas.
rootCause: A misconfigured Horizontal Pod Autoscaler set minReplicas to 0, so the order-consumer scaled all the way down to zero replicas during a low-traffic window and never scaled back up, leaving the queue with no consumers.
resolution: Set the consumer deployment back to a minimum of 3 replicas (corrected HPA minReplicas) and scaled it up immediately. Consumers re-attached to the queue and drained the 51k backlog in a few minutes; no messages were lost because they were still queued.
prevention: Alert on RabbitMQ queue depth AND on consumers=0 for any critical queue. Enforce a minimum replica floor (minReplicas >= 1) for stateful consumers and add a guardrail/policy check on HPA configs. Add a synthetic 'heartbeat' message to verify end-to-end processing continuously.

title: Poison message loops and floods the Dead Letter Queue, stalling processing
problem: The notifications consumer stopped making progress and the Dead Letter Queue filled rapidly. A single malformed message was being redelivered in a loop, repeatedly crashing the handler and pushing both the main queue and DLQ into an error spiral.
symptoms: Throughput on notifications.process drops to near zero. The DLQ count climbs into the tens of thousands. The consumer logs the same deserialization exception over and over with the same message ID. Legitimate notifications are delayed for all users.
logs:
2026-06-17T14:20:01Z [notif-consumer] ERROR Failed to process message id=msg-7c41 deliveryTag=1882
2026-06-17T14:20:01Z [notif-consumer] ERROR com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.exc.MismatchedInputException: Cannot deserialize value of type `int` from String "N/A"
2026-06-17T14:20:01Z [notif-consumer]   at NotificationPayload.userId(NotificationPayload.java:34)
2026-06-17T14:20:01Z [notif-consumer] WARN  nack with requeue=true id=msg-7c41 (redelivered=true count=4127)
2026-06-17T14:20:02Z [rabbitmq] queue=notifications.process redeliver_rate=310/s
2026-06-17T14:20:02Z [rabbitmq] queue=notifications.dlq messages_ready=24190 growing
investigationSteps: Checked queue metrics and saw the main queue redeliver_rate spiking and the DLQ growing fast — a sign of repeated failure rather than a volume spike.
Read the consumer logs and found the same message ID (msg-7c41) failing repeatedly with a Jackson deserialization error (userId field contained the string 'N/A').
Noted redelivered=true with a very high delivery count, confirming the message was being nacked with requeue=true and looping back to the consumer.
Inspected the message payload from the DLQ and confirmed it was malformed at the source — a producer had emitted userId as 'N/A' instead of an integer.
Reviewed the consumer's error handling and found it requeued on any exception with no retry cap and no parking of poison messages, which created the infinite loop.
Confirmed the legitimate messages behind the poison message were starved because the consumer kept re-picking the failing one.
rootCause: A malformed 'poison' message (userId='N/A' instead of an integer) could not be deserialized, and the consumer was configured to nack-with-requeue on all errors with no retry limit, so the message looped infinitely, blocked the queue, and flooded the DLQ.
resolution: Removed/parked the poison message and corrected the consumer to nack with requeue=false (route to DLQ) after a bounded retry count, so it stopped looping. Fixed the upstream producer to send a valid integer (or null), then replayed the valid DLQ messages back to the main queue after deploying the fix.
prevention: Implement a bounded retry policy with a max-delivery count and automatic dead-lettering of poison messages. Validate payloads against a schema at the producer. Alert on DLQ growth and on high redelivery rates. Add a DLQ replay tool and dashboards for redelivery counts.

title: Bad deploy causes site-wide 500 errors; rolled back to restore service
problem: Immediately after the 15:30 release, the website began throwing HTTP 500 errors across nearly every page. The error rate jumped from baseline to over 80% of requests within two minutes of the rollout completing.
symptoms: Customers see a generic error page on most actions. The error-rate dashboard spikes vertically at 15:31. Successful request volume collapses. The spike lines up exactly with the deployment marker; the previous version had been stable for days.
logs:
2026-06-17T15:30:58Z [deploy] release v4.12.0 rollout complete (replicas 6/6 updated)
2026-06-17T15:31:04Z [web] ERROR Uncaught exception handling GET /  -> 500
2026-06-17T15:31:04Z [web] ERROR NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "FeatureClient.isEnabled(String)" because "this.featureClient" is null
2026-06-17T15:31:04Z [web]   at HomeController.index(HomeController.java:58)
2026-06-17T15:31:05Z [gateway] 500 rate=82% (was 0.4%) window=1m
2026-06-17T15:31:20Z [deploy] alert: error_rate SLO breached, version=v4.12.0
investigationSteps: Looked at the error-rate timeline and saw a sharp spike beginning seconds after the v4.12.0 rollout completed — strong correlation with the deploy.
Confirmed the spike is site-wide (multiple endpoints, not one feature) and that the prior version had a flat, healthy error rate.
Read the application logs and found a consistent NullPointerException on a newly added FeatureClient dependency that was null at runtime.
Checked the diff in v4.12.0 and saw a new dependency was added but its bean/dependency injection wiring was incomplete, so it was never initialized.
Determined the issue affected the common request path (home/index and shared controller), explaining the broad blast radius.
Made the call to roll back rather than hot-fix forward, given the severity and clear correlation to the release.
rootCause: Release v4.12.0 introduced a new FeatureClient dependency that was not wired/initialized correctly (null at runtime), causing a NullPointerException on a shared code path and producing site-wide HTTP 500s.
resolution: Rolled back the deployment to the previous stable version (v4.11.3), which restored service within minutes. The faulty wiring was fixed in code, tested, and re-released later with verification in staging.
prevention: Use progressive/canary rollouts with automatic rollback on SLO breach so a bad release affects only a small slice. Add a smoke test that hits key endpoints post-deploy before shifting full traffic. Improve test coverage for dependency-injection wiring and require staging verification before production releases.

title: Missing records in daily report after an overnight ETL job failed silently
problem: Business users reported that the daily sales report was missing all of yesterday's transactions. The overnight ETL job that loads transactions into the reporting warehouse had failed, but it exited without raising an alert, so the failure went unnoticed until morning.
symptoms: The report shows data only up to two days ago; yesterday's rows are entirely absent. The UI dashboards built on the warehouse show a flat line for the missing day. No alert or ticket was generated overnight. Source operational database clearly contains yesterday's transactions.
logs:
2026-06-17T02:00:01Z [etl] INFO  Starting job daily_sales_load run_id=20260617-0200
2026-06-17T02:00:05Z [etl] INFO  Extract source=ops_db rows=184502
2026-06-17T02:03:48Z [etl] ERROR Load step failed: ORA-12541: TNS:no listener (warehouse)
2026-06-17T02:03:48Z [etl] ERROR Transform/load aborted after 0 rows loaded
2026-06-17T02:03:48Z [etl] INFO  Job daily_sales_load finished exit_code=0 status=COMPLETED
2026-06-17T02:03:48Z [scheduler] daily_sales_load run_id=20260617-0200 result=SUCCESS
investigationSteps: Compared the source operational DB with the warehouse and confirmed yesterday's transactions exist in the source but are missing in the reporting tables — the gap is in the load, not the source.
Located last night's ETL run and read its logs; the extract succeeded (184,502 rows) but the load step failed with ORA-12541 (warehouse listener down at that moment).
Spotted the critical defect: despite the load error, the job logged status=COMPLETED with exit_code=0, so the scheduler recorded SUCCESS and no alert fired.
Checked why the warehouse was unreachable at 02:03 and found it overlapped a brief maintenance window/restart on the warehouse listener.
Reviewed the ETL error handling and confirmed exceptions in the load step were caught and swallowed without propagating a non-zero exit code.
Confirmed no data was corrupted — the load simply never ran for that day, so a re-run would backfill cleanly.
rootCause: The ETL load step failed because the warehouse listener was briefly down, but the job swallowed the exception and exited with code 0 (status COMPLETED), so the scheduler reported success and no failure alert was raised — a silent failure that left a one-day data gap.
resolution: Re-ran the ETL job for the missing date once the warehouse was confirmed available; the 184k rows loaded and the report/dashboards backfilled correctly. The job was patched to propagate the real exit code on any step failure.
prevention: Fix error handling so failed steps return a non-zero exit code and fail the job. Add alerting on job failures AND data-freshness/row-count checks (alert if today's expected rows are missing). Add retries with backoff for transient warehouse connectivity, and reconcile source-vs-warehouse counts after each load.

title: Stale/wrong data shown to users after Redis cache outage
problem: Users started seeing outdated product prices and inventory counts. The Redis cache cluster became unavailable, and the application both failed to refresh cached values and, in some paths, kept serving expired entries, so customers saw stale data.
symptoms: Product pages show prices and stock levels that no longer match the database. Some requests are slow as they fall back to the database; others return clearly old values. Redis client logs show connection timeouts. The primary database itself is healthy and has correct, current data.
logs:
2026-06-17T16:12:03Z [catalog] WARN  Redis GET product:88231 timed out after 2000ms
2026-06-17T16:12:03Z [catalog] ERROR redis.clients.jedis.exceptions.JedisConnectionException: Could not get a resource from the pool
2026-06-17T16:12:03Z [catalog] WARN  Cache unavailable, serving last-known value from local in-process cache (age=3h)
2026-06-17T16:12:05Z [redis] node 10.0.4.21:6379 state=fail (primary down, no failover quorum)
2026-06-17T16:12:05Z [redis] cluster_state:fail cluster_slots_ok:9000 cluster_slots_fail:7384
2026-06-17T16:12:10Z [catalog] INFO  DB fallback latency p95=410ms (was 35ms cached)
investigationSteps: Confirmed the database holds correct, current values, so the problem is in the caching layer, not the source of truth.
Read the catalog service logs and found Redis connection timeouts and JedisConnectionException — the app cannot reach the cache.
Checked the Redis cluster state and found a primary node down with cluster_state:fail and many slots failing (no failover quorum reached).
Identified the user-visible stale data came from a long-lived in-process fallback cache (age 3h) that the app served when Redis was unreachable, with too-long TTLs.
Verified increased DB fallback latency (p95 410ms vs 35ms cached), explaining the partial slowdown alongside the staleness.
Correlated the Redis node failure with an infrastructure event and confirmed automatic failover had not completed due to lost quorum.
rootCause: A Redis primary node failed and the cluster could not complete failover (no quorum), so the application lost its cache. The app then served stale values from an in-process fallback cache with overly long TTLs, surfacing outdated prices and inventory to users.
resolution: Restored Redis cluster quorum by bringing the failed node/replica back and promoting a replica to primary, which re-enabled normal caching. As mitigation, the stale in-process fallback TTL was shortened and the affected keys were invalidated so fresh values reloaded from the database.
prevention: Run Redis with replicas and enough nodes for reliable automatic failover, and alert on cluster_state and node health. Bound fallback-cache TTLs and prefer 'serve from DB' over serving very stale data for price/inventory. Add cache hit-rate and staleness monitoring and a documented cache-failover runbook.

title: Gradual slowdown and OOM crashes from an application memory leak
problem: A backend service slowed down over the course of each day and then crashed with out-of-memory errors, recovering only when restarted. The pattern repeated daily, with response times degrading as heap usage climbed toward the limit.
symptoms: Latency creeps up over hours; garbage-collection pauses lengthen. The service eventually OOM-kills and restarts, briefly restoring performance. Heap usage shows a sawtooth that trends upward and never returns to baseline. Restarts 'fix' it temporarily, so it was initially mistaken for capacity.
logs:
2026-06-17T18:44:12Z [svc] WARN  GC pause Full GC 4123ms, heap 7.6G/8G after collection
2026-06-17T18:45:01Z [svc] WARN  Allocation stall, old gen 96% occupied
2026-06-17T18:46:33Z [svc] ERROR java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
2026-06-17T18:46:33Z [svc]   at SessionRegistry.put(SessionRegistry.java:71)
2026-06-17T18:46:34Z [k8s] svc pod OOMKilled, restartCount=5, lastState.reason=OOMKilled
2026-06-17T18:46:40Z [svc] INFO  Process restarted, heap 0.4G/8G (baseline restored)
2026-06-17T18:46:40Z [heap-dump] dominator: java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap retained=6.9G entries=4.1M (SessionRegistry.cache)
investigationSteps: Reviewed long-term metrics and confirmed a daily pattern of rising heap and latency culminating in OOM, with restarts only temporarily restoring baseline — symptomatic of a leak rather than a load spike.
Checked traffic volume and found it was roughly flat day over day, so growth in memory was not explained by increased demand.
Read the logs and confirmed OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space and repeated OOMKilled restarts (restartCount climbing).
Captured/inspected a heap dump and identified the dominator: a ConcurrentHashMap in SessionRegistry retaining ~6.9G across 4.1M entries.
Examined SessionRegistry and found entries were added on each session but never evicted/removed when sessions ended — an unbounded cache.
Correlated the leak's introduction with a recent change that added the session cache without a size bound or expiry, confirming root cause.
rootCause: An unbounded in-memory cache (SessionRegistry's ConcurrentHashMap) accumulated session entries that were never evicted or expired, so heap usage grew continuously until the JVM exhausted memory and was OOM-killed.
resolution: Replaced the unbounded map with a bounded cache with size limits and time-based eviction (and ensured entries are removed on session end), eliminating the leak. A rolling restart provided immediate relief while the fix was deployed and validated under load.
prevention: Alert on heap-usage trend and OOMKilled restart counts, not just on crashes. Run periodic load/soak tests to catch leaks before production. Enforce bounded caches with eviction policies as a coding standard, and review heap dumps as part of memory-related incident runbooks.

title: Payments failing due to third-party gateway outage; coordinating support comms
problem: Customers could not complete payments at checkout. Our service was healthy, but the third-party payment gateway was returning errors and timeouts, so all charge attempts failed. The incident also required clear, timely communication to customers and stakeholders.
symptoms: Checkout fails at the payment step with a generic 'payment could not be processed' message. Order placement drops sharply. Our payment service logs show gateway 503s and timeouts. The gateway provider's status page reports a major incident affecting card processing.
