2026-06-17T19:05:22Z [payments] INFO  Submitting charge orderId=90112 amount=49.99 to gateway
2026-06-17T19:05:52Z [payments] ERROR Gateway call failed: 503 Service Unavailable provider=acme-pay
2026-06-17T19:05:52Z [payments] ERROR upstream timeout after 30000ms endpoint=POST https://api.acme-pay.com/v2/charges
2026-06-17T19:05:52Z [payments] WARN  charge declined upstream, marking order PAYMENT_FAILED orderId=90112
2026-06-17T19:06:00Z [payments] metrics gateway_error_rate=100% success=0 over 5m
2026-06-17T19:06:30Z [statuspage] acme-pay: "Investigating elevated errors on card charges" severity=major
investigationSteps: Confirmed our payment service and the rest of the site are healthy; only the charge step is failing, isolating the problem to payments.
Read the payment service logs and saw 100% of charge attempts returning gateway 503s/timeouts from provider acme-pay.
Checked the gateway provider's public status page and confirmed they had declared a major incident on card processing — an external, provider-side outage.
Verified our credentials, request format, and recent changes to rule out a config or integration regression on our side (no recent deploy; requests are well-formed).
Assessed customer impact: failed orders are correctly marked PAYMENT_FAILED with no duplicate charges, so no money was taken erroneously.
Initiated incident comms: posted a status update to customers, notified stakeholders, and opened a ticket with the provider while monitoring their status page for recovery.
rootCause: A major outage at the third-party payment gateway (provider-side) caused all charge requests to return 503s and timeouts. The failure was entirely external; our integration and configuration were correct.
resolution: There was no code fix on our side; we monitored the provider until their service recovered, after which charges succeeded again. During the outage we communicated clearly to customers (a banner and support messaging) and confirmed no duplicate charges occurred; affected customers were invited to retry once service was restored.
prevention: Subscribe to the provider's status/webhook alerts and alert on payment success-rate drops. Prepare pre-written incident-communication templates and a customer-facing status banner. Evaluate a secondary/failover payment provider and implement idempotency keys and safe retry/queueing so transient gateway errors don't cause lost or duplicate charges.

title: Feature works in staging but fails in production due to configuration drift
problem: A newly released document-export feature worked perfectly in staging but failed every time in production. The code was identical; the difference was environment configuration — a missing environment variable and a stale endpoint pointing the production service at the wrong storage host.
symptoms: In production, clicking 'Export' returns an error and no file is produced; in staging the same action succeeds. Production logs show authentication/connection failures to a storage service. No code differs between environments; only the behavior differs by environment.
logs:
2026-06-17T20:15:09Z [export-svc][prod] INFO  Export requested docId=5521 format=pdf
2026-06-17T20:15:09Z [export-svc][prod] ERROR Missing required env var STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY (null)
2026-06-17T20:15:09Z [export-svc][prod] ERROR Failed to init storage client; falling back to default endpoint
2026-06-17T20:15:10Z [export-svc][prod] ERROR Connection refused to storage endpoint=https://staging-files.internal:443
2026-06-17T20:15:10Z [export-svc][prod] WARN  Export failed docId=5521 reason=storage_unavailable
2026-06-17T20:14:50Z [export-svc][staging] INFO  Export succeeded docId=5521 endpoint=https://staging-files.internal:443 key=present
investigationSteps: Confirmed the deployed code/version is identical in staging and production, so the difference must be environmental rather than a code regression.
Reproduced the failure in production and read the logs, which showed a missing STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY env var (null) at startup.
Noticed production then 'fell back' to a default endpoint and tried to reach https://staging-files.internal — the wrong, staging-only storage host — and got connection refused.
Compared environment configuration between staging and production and found production was missing the access-key variable and had a stale/incorrect storage endpoint baked into the default.
Checked how config is managed and found these values were set manually in staging but never added to the production config (drift introduced during rollout).
Verified the production storage service itself was reachable when pointed at the correct production endpoint with valid credentials, confirming config — not the storage service — was the cause.
rootCause: Configuration drift between environments: the production deployment was missing the STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY environment variable and used a stale default endpoint pointing at the staging storage host, so the export feature could not authenticate or reach the correct storage in production.
resolution: Added the missing STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY to the production configuration and corrected the storage endpoint to the production host, then restarted the export service. Exports succeeded immediately in production.
prevention: Manage configuration as code with the same source-of-truth across environments and diff staging vs production in CI. Validate required environment variables at startup (fail fast instead of falling back to a wrong default). Remove environment-specific defaults from code, and add a post-deploy config/health check that verifies connectivity to the correct dependencies.

title: 3am Alert Storm — One Root Cause Buried Under Hundreds of Alerts
problem: At 03:07 the on-call engineer was paged by a flood of ~340 alerts across dozens of services within four minutes. The volume made it impossible to tell what was actually broken versus what was downstream noise.
symptoms: PagerDuty incident count spiked from 0 to 340+ in under 5 minutes. Alerts spanned checkout, search, recommendations, notifications, and the API gateway. Almost all were 'HTTP 5xx ratio high' or 'health check failing'. A single earlier alert at 03:06:12 fired for the primary PostgreSQL database before everything else.
logs:
03:06:12 CRIT [db-primary] alert=PostgresDown msg="could not connect: FATAL: the database system is in recovery mode"
03:06:48 WARN [checkout-svc] alert=HTTP5xxRatioHigh value=0.61 threshold=0.05
03:06:49 WARN [search-svc] alert=HTTP5xxRatioHigh value=0.58 threshold=0.05
03:06:50 WARN [recommendations-svc] alert=DependencyTimeout target=db-primary
03:06:51 WARN [notifications-svc] alert=HealthCheckFailing endpoint=/healthz
03:07:02 WARN [api-gateway] alert=UpstreamErrorsHigh value=0.55 threshold=0.10
... (332 more downstream alerts) ...
db-primary log: 03:05:58 PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/000000010000002A0000007F": No space left on device
db-primary log: 03:06:01 LOG: database system is shut down
db-primary log: 03:06:05 LOG: database system was interrupted; entering recovery
investigationSteps: Sort alerts by first-fired timestamp instead of by severity; the earliest alert (PostgresDown at 03:06:12) precedes the wave of 5xx alerts by 30+ seconds, making it the prime suspect.
Build a dependency view: nearly every screaming service (checkout, search, recommendations, notifications) shares one common downstream — db-primary.
Confirm correlation, not coincidence: each downstream alert text references db-primary timeouts or connection failures, not independent faults.
Pull db-primary logs and find the PANIC at 03:05:58 — 'No space left on device' on the pg_wal partition, which triggered shutdown then recovery mode.
Verify disk: df shows /var/lib/postgresql/pg_wal at 100% due to WAL accumulation from a stuck replication slot.
Confirm the hypothesis by silencing/grouping: treat the 339 downstream alerts as symptoms of the single root alert and focus remediation on the database disk.
rootCause: An inactive logical replication slot stopped consuming WAL, so WAL segments accumulated until the pg_wal filesystem hit 100%. PostgreSQL could not write WAL, panicked, shut down, and entered crash recovery — taking every dependent service offline and generating a downstream alert storm.
resolution: Dropped the orphaned replication slot, freeing WAL recycling; extended the pg_wal volume by 50GB to clear the immediate full condition; PostgreSQL finished recovery and accepted connections, after which all downstream 5xx alerts auto-resolved within two minutes.
prevention: Add alert correlation/grouping in the alerting tool keyed by shared dependency so a database outage rolls up into one incident instead of 340. Add a disk-usage alert on pg_wal at 75% and 90% (well before saturation), monitor replication-slot lag/retained WAL, and add a watchdog to drop or warn on inactive slots. Define alert dependency suppression so downstream health-check alerts are muted when an upstream root alert is firing.

title: Flapping False-Positive Alert Erodes On-Call Trust
problem: A 'p95 latency high' alert on the payments API fired and self-resolved dozens of times per day, always clearing within a minute. On-call started ignoring it, risking a real incident being missed (alert fatigue).
symptoms: Same alert opened and closed 40+ times in 24 hours, almost always resolving in under 60 seconds. Each firing showed a brief p95 spike to ~310ms against a 300ms threshold, then back to ~120ms. No customer complaints, no error-rate change, no correlated saturation.
logs:
07:14:03 ALERT firing  name=PaymentsP95High value=312ms threshold=300ms for=0s
07:14:51 ALERT resolved name=PaymentsP95High value=118ms
07:31:22 ALERT firing  name=PaymentsP95High value=305ms threshold=300ms for=0s
07:31:48 ALERT resolved name=PaymentsP95High value=121ms
08:02:10 ALERT firing  name=PaymentsP95High value=327ms threshold=300ms for=0s
08:02:39 ALERT resolved name=PaymentsP95High value=109ms
metrics: payments_request_duration_seconds p50=0.090 p95=0.125 p99=0.240 (steady)
note: spikes align with cron 'token-refresh' every ~15-20m causing a single slow request
investigationSteps: Quantify the flapping: count firing/resolved pairs and median time-to-resolve (under 60s) to confirm this is threshold flapping, not a sustained problem.
Inspect the metric: p50/p95/p99 are stable except for momentary single-sample spikes barely crossing 300ms — classic too-tight threshold with no duration window.
Check the alert rule: it triggers on an instantaneous breach (for: 0s) with no sustained-duration requirement, so any transient blip pages.
Correlate spikes with events: each spike lines up with a periodic token-refresh job that makes one cold-cache request slightly slower; impact is negligible.
Confirm there is no real degradation: error rate, saturation, and customer success metrics are flat throughout the flapping window.
rootCause: The alert threshold (300ms) sat right on top of normal p95 variance and used an instantaneous trigger with no duration/'for' window, so transient single-request blips from a periodic token-refresh job repeatedly tripped it — a false-positive flap rather than a genuine latency regression.
resolution: Raised the threshold to a value above observed normal variance (450ms) and added a sustained-duration condition (must breach for 5 minutes) plus hysteresis so it only resolves once well below threshold. The alert stopped flapping immediately while still catching genuine sustained latency.
prevention: Set thresholds from historical percentile distributions (e.g., threshold above the 99th-percentile-of-p95 over weeks), not round numbers. Require a 'for' duration so transient spikes are ignored, add hysteresis (separate fire/clear levels) to stop flapping, and route low-actionability alerts to a dashboard/ticket rather than a page. Periodically review alert noise and tune or delete non-actionable alerts.

title: Gradual Degradation Over Days — File Descriptor Leak Ends in Outage
problem: A reporting microservice that ran fine after each deploy slowly degraded over four to five days and then crashed with 'too many open files', taking the service down until it was restarted.
symptoms: Latency and error rate crept upward day over day with no traffic change. The crash coincided with the open file-descriptor count reaching the process ulimit (4096). Restarting the pod reset everything to healthy — for another few days.
logs:
day1 12:00 fd_open=180  p99=140ms errors=0.0%
day3 12:00 fd_open=1900 p99=260ms errors=0.3%
day5 09:40 fd_open=4090 p99=900ms errors=4.1%
day5 09:48 ERROR accept: too many open files
day5 09:48 ERROR java.net.SocketException: Too many open files
day5 09:49 ERROR HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available; request timed out after 30000ms
$ lsof -p 8123 | wc -l
4093
$ lsof -p 8123 | grep -c 'CLOSE_WAIT'
3771
metric: process_open_fds slope ≈ +650/day, monotonic, never decreasing
investigationSteps: Plot process_open_fds over a week — a monotonic, never-decreasing climb is the signature of a leak rather than load.
Correlate the crash time with fd_open hitting the 4096 ulimit and the 'too many open files' errors — saturation of a finite resource (USE method: Utilization at 100%).
Use lsof on the PID; thousands of sockets stuck in CLOSE_WAIT mean the app accepts/opens connections but never closes them.
Trace which code path opens those sockets: they map to an outbound HTTP client used by the report-export feature.
Review that client's usage and find responses/streams are read but the HttpClient response body (and thus the socket) is never closed, leaking one fd per export call.
Confirm by reproducing in staging: hammering the export endpoint reproduces the linear fd growth, and adding a close() flattens the curve.
rootCause: The report-export code path created HTTP client connections (and their response input streams) that were never explicitly closed, leaking one file descriptor per call. Over days these accumulated as CLOSE_WAIT sockets until the process hit its file-descriptor ulimit and could no longer accept connections or open DB sockets.
resolution: Wrapped the HTTP response/stream in a try-with-resources (ensuring close()) and switched to a pooled, properly-released client. Deployed the fix; fd count stabilized at ~200 and stopped climbing. Restarted the affected pod to clear the leaked descriptors immediately.
prevention: Add a monotonic-growth alert on process_open_fds (warn at 50% of ulimit, page at 80%) so leaks are caught days before saturation. Add connection-pool and CLOSE_WAIT socket metrics to dashboards. Enforce resource cleanup via static analysis/linters for unclosed Closeables, raise ulimits as a safety margin (not a fix), and add a soak/endurance test in CI that runs the service under sustained load to surface slow leaks.

title: Peak-Traffic Saturation — Thread Pool Maxed, Latency Climbs
problem: Every weekday at the lunchtime traffic peak, the order API's latency climbed sharply and a fraction of requests timed out, even though CPU on the hosts looked only moderately busy. Off-peak it was perfectly healthy.
symptoms: p99 latency rose from ~150ms to ~3.5s during the peak; request queue depth and active thread count pinned at the configured maximum; a small percentage of requests returned 503/timeout. The golden signal that screamed was saturation (queue length), not raw errors.
logs:
12:00 rps=1200 active_threads=40/40 queue_depth=0   p99=160ms cpu=55%
12:25 rps=2600 active_threads=40/40 queue_depth=210 p99=1800ms cpu=72%
12:40 rps=3100 active_threads=40/40 queue_depth=540 p99=3500ms cpu=78% 503s=2.3%
log: 12:40:11 WARN tomcat-exec pool exhausted: maxThreads=40 currentBusy=40 acceptCount queue=540
log: 12:40:12 ERROR request timed out after 3000ms waiting for worker thread
threaddump: 38/40 worker threads BLOCKED in jdbc call awaiting connection from HikariPool (max=20)
metric: db_pool_active=20/20 db_pool_pending=33
investigationSteps: Apply the USE method to peak: utilization of the worker thread pool is 100% (40/40 busy) with a growing run queue — saturation, the textbook latency-under-load signal.
Note CPU is only ~78% — the bottleneck is not CPU; threads are waiting, not computing.
Take a thread dump during the peak: most worker threads are BLOCKED waiting on a JDBC connection, pointing one level deeper.
Inspect the DB connection pool: db_pool_active=20/20 with 33 requests pending — the connection pool (max 20) is the true constraint behind the thread pool.
Correlate timeline: queue_depth and p99 rise together exactly as rps crosses ~2500, confirming demand exceeds provisioned concurrency at peak only.
Validate capacity math: with 20 DB connections and per-query time, max sustainable throughput is well below the peak rps, explaining the queue buildup.
rootCause: At peak the request rate exceeded the service's provisioned concurrency. Worker threads saturated because they were all blocked waiting on an undersized database connection pool (max 20). The result was queue buildup, climbing latency, and timeout-driven 503s — a saturation incident, not a code error.
resolution: Increased the DB connection pool to a size matched to DB capacity and tuned the worker thread pool accordingly, then enabled horizontal autoscaling on queue depth so extra replicas spin up at peak. After tuning, peak p99 dropped back to ~200ms with zero 503s.
prevention: Alert on saturation signals (thread-pool utilization, queue depth, db_pool_pending) rather than only on errors/latency, since saturation precedes failure. Right-size pools via load testing to find the knee of the latency curve, add horizontal autoscaling keyed to a leading saturation metric, set sensible timeouts/back-pressure, and run regular peak-load capacity tests so headroom is verified before real peaks.

title: Cascading Failure — One Slow Service Drags Down the Whole Platform
problem: A slowdown in a single non-critical recommendations service rippled outward and brought down checkout and the home page within minutes. There was no circuit breaker, so callers blocked on the slow dependency and exhausted their own resources.
symptoms: Recommendations latency rose first, then upstream services (product-page, checkout) saw their own thread pools fill and start returning 5xx. Failure spread upstream in a wave; the whole site became unavailable even though only one minor backend had originally degraded.
logs:
14:02 recommendations-svc p99=4200ms (normal ~120ms) cause=GC pause / slow downstream
14:03 product-page-svc threads=200/200 busy waiting on recommendations call (timeout=30s)
14:04 product-page-svc p99=29s errors=48% msg="upstream recommendations timed out"
14:05 checkout-svc threads=200/200 busy (calls product-page for cart upsell)
14:06 api-gateway 5xx_ratio=0.71 msg="upstream unavailable"
log: 14:04:55 ERROR no available worker threads; all blocked on synchronous call to recommendations
log: NOTE clients use default 30s timeout, no circuit breaker, no fallback, unbounded retries
trace: home-page -> product-page -> recommendations (4.2s) with retries x3 = ~12s blocked per request
investigationSteps: Reconstruct the failure order from timestamps: recommendations degraded first (14:02), then product-page (14:03-04), then checkout (14:05), then gateway (14:06) — failure propagated upstream, the signature of a cascade.
Use distributed traces to find the common slow span: every failing upstream request spends ~4s+ blocked in a synchronous call to recommendations.
Inspect thread pools of the upstream services: they are 100% busy, all threads parked waiting on the slow recommendations call rather than doing work.
Check client configuration: 30s timeouts, no circuit breaker, no fallback, and retries that multiply load on the already-struggling dependency.
Identify the original trigger: a long GC pause / slow query on recommendations raised its latency; without isolation this back-pressured every caller.
Confirm the amplification: retries against the slow service increased its load further, deepening the cascade (positive feedback loop).
rootCause: A latency spike in a single downstream service propagated because callers made synchronous calls with long timeouts, no circuit breaker, no fallback, and aggressive retries. Upstream thread pools filled with threads blocked on the slow dependency, so a minor backend slowdown cascaded into a full platform outage.
resolution: Stabilized recommendations (cleared the GC/slow-query trigger and restarted affected pods) to break the immediate cascade, then shipped resilience: circuit breakers around the recommendations call, short timeouts, a graceful fallback (render the page without recommendations), and bounded retries with backoff. Recovery was immediate once callers stopped blocking.
prevention: Wrap all inter-service calls in circuit breakers with sensible timeouts and bulkheads so one dependency cannot consume all caller threads. Make non-critical dependencies (like recommendations) optional with graceful degradation/fallbacks. Use bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter to avoid retry storms, add load shedding/back-pressure, and run dependency failure (chaos) drills to verify isolation.

title: Intermittent Auth/Cert Failures Caused by NTP Clock Skew
problem: Service-to-service authentication and TLS/JWT validation failed intermittently — roughly on a subset of hosts — with errors about tokens 'not yet valid' or 'expired'. The failures came and went and didn't correlate with deploys or load.
symptoms: Sporadic 401/invalid-token responses concentrated on a few hosts; mTLS handshakes occasionally rejected as 'certificate not yet valid'. Retrying often succeeded a moment later. The affected nodes shared no app version — only that their system clocks were drifting.
logs:
node-7 10:00:03 ERROR JWT validation failed: token used before issued (iat=1718614805 now=1718614763) clock skew?
node-7 10:00:05 ERROR TLS handshake: certificate is not yet valid: notBefore=10:00:04 systemTime=10:00:01
node-3 10:00:04 ERROR JWT expired 39s ago (exp in past relative to local clock)
$ chronyc tracking (node-7)
Last offset     : +43.812s
Leap status     : Not synchronised
$ timedatectl (node-7)
NTP service: inactive
System clock synchronized: no
$ for h in node-1..node-9; do ssh $h date +%s; done -> spread of ~44s across hosts
investigationSteps: Group failures by host: errors cluster on node-3 and node-7, not on a service version or deploy — pointing to host-level state rather than code.
Read the error text carefully: 'token used before issued', 'expired', and 'certificate not yet valid' are all time-comparison failures, hinting at clock disagreement.
Compare wall-clock across hosts (date +%s in a loop): the fleet spans ~44 seconds of skew, far beyond normal token/cert validity tolerances.
Check time sync on the bad nodes: chronyc/timedatectl show 'Not synchronised', NTP inactive, and a +43s offset on node-7.

Map skew to symptom: a node running 40+ seconds fast/slow will reject freshly-issued tokens (not yet valid) or treat valid ones as expired, exactly matching the intermittent 401s and handshake rejects.
Confirm by correcting one node's clock and re-testing: auth and TLS validation immediately stop failing on that host.
rootCause: NTP/chrony was not running (or was failing to reach its time source) on a subset of hosts, letting their system clocks drift tens of seconds out of sync with the rest of the fleet. Because JWT iat/exp and X.509 notBefore/notAfter are validated against local time, the skewed nodes intermittently rejected valid tokens and certificates.
resolution: Re-enabled and restarted chrony on the affected hosts, pointed them at the internal NTP servers, and force-stepped the clocks back into sync. Once offsets fell under a second, the intermittent 401s and TLS 'not yet valid' errors stopped. Verified all nodes reported 'System clock synchronized: yes'.
prevention: Monitor and alert on clock offset per host (e.g., chrony offset > 250ms) and on 'NTP not synchronised' status across the fleet. Ensure the time-sync daemon is managed/started at boot via config management and reaches reliable NTP/PTP sources. Add a small clock-skew tolerance (leeway) to JWT/cert validation where appropriate, and include clock-sync checks in host health/readiness probes.

title: High Time-To-First-Byte from Slow TLS Handshakes Under Load
problem: Under traffic peaks, users experienced slow page starts: time-to-first-byte (TTFB) climbed sharply while the application's own server-side processing time stayed flat. The slowness was in connection setup, not in generating the response.
symptoms: p95 TTFB jumped from ~90ms to ~1.6s at peak, but backend request_duration stayed ~80ms. The gap was in TLS handshake time. New connections were slow; reused (keep-alive) connections were fast. CPU on the TLS-terminating layer spiked during peaks.
logs:
peak 19:30: ttfb_p95=1620ms backend_request_p95=82ms  (delta ~1.5s in connect/TLS)
nginx log: $request_time=1.610 $upstream_response_time=0.079 $ssl_handshake_time=1.420
metric: ssl_handshakes_per_sec=4200 (off-peak ~300) tls_session_reuse_ratio=0.06
cpu (lb-tls-1): 96% sys, perf top -> RSA private key operations dominating
client note: many short-lived connections, no HTTP keep-alive, full handshake every request
config: ssl_session_cache off; ssl_session_tickets off; RSA-2048 key, no ECDHE session resumption
investigationSteps: Decompose TTFB: total request_time (1.61s) minus upstream_response_time (0.08s) leaves ~1.5s spent before the app — localize the latency to connection/TLS, not application code.
Read the handshake metric: ssl_handshake_time ~1.42s confirms TLS negotiation is the dominant cost.
Check connection reuse: tls_session_reuse_ratio is only 6% and keep-alive is effectively off, so nearly every request pays a full handshake at peak.
Profile the TLS terminator's CPU: it is pinned at ~96% doing RSA private-key operations — the asymmetric crypto of full handshakes is saturating CPU.
Correlate with load: ssl_handshakes_per_sec rises from ~300 to ~4200 at peak, exactly tracking the TTFB spike (more new handshakes -> more CPU contention -> slower handshakes).
Inspect TLS config and find session resumption disabled (no session cache, no tickets), forcing expensive full handshakes repeatedly.
rootCause: Under peak load the TLS-terminating layer was overwhelmed by full handshakes: session resumption was disabled and clients used short-lived connections with no keep-alive, so every request triggered a fresh, CPU-expensive RSA handshake. The crypto work saturated CPU, which slowed handshakes further and inflated TTFB while backend processing stayed fast.
resolution: Enabled TLS session resumption (session cache + tickets) and HTTP keep-alive so most requests skip the full handshake, switched the cipher preference to ECDHE and enabled hardware/AES-NI acceleration, and added more TLS-terminator capacity. TTFB at peak fell back to ~120ms with handshake CPU well under control.
prevention: Monitor TTFB and decompose it (connect/TLS vs upstream) so connection-setup latency is visible separately from app latency. Alert on ssl_handshakes_per_sec, TLS reuse ratio, and TLS-terminator CPU. Keep session resumption and keep-alive enabled, prefer efficient cipher suites with hardware acceleration, offload TLS to right-sized/scalable terminators, and include TLS handshake load in capacity tests.

title: Nightly Batch Job Overruns Into Business Hours, Holding DB Locks
problem: A nightly ETL/batch job that normally finished before 06:00 began overrunning into the workday. While it ran, the customer-facing app slowed dramatically because a long-running transaction held locks on tables the app needed.
symptoms: After 08:00 the app showed climbing latency and statement timeouts. DB lock-wait counts and 'blocked queries' spiked. The blocking session was the batch job's single giant transaction. The batch start time had quietly drifted later as data volume grew.
logs:
06:00 expected batch finish — actual finish 09:18 (overran by ~3h)
db log: 08:05:11 LOG: process 4412 still waiting for ShareLock on transaction 998877 after 5000.102 ms
db log: 08:05:11 DETAIL: blocked by process 3120 (batch_etl) holding lock on relation "orders"
db log: 08:06:02 ERROR: canceling statement due to statement timeout (app query on orders)
pg_stat_activity: pid=3120 state=active query="UPDATE orders SET ... " xact_start=02:40 (running 5h28m)
metric: app_p99=2900ms during 08:00-09:18, ~150ms otherwise; lock_waits=hundreds/min
note: batch wraps the entire 40M-row update in one transaction, no batching/commits
investigationSteps: Correlate the app slowdown window (08:00-09:18) with an external event rather than app changes; it matches exactly when the batch job is still running.
Check DB lock metrics: hundreds of lock-waits per minute and many 'blocked' queries appear only during that window.
Find the blocker via pg_stat_activity / lock views: the blocking PID is the batch_etl session with an xact_start hours earlier — one enormous long-running transaction.
Read the lock detail: app queries are waiting on ShareLock of the orders table held by the batch update, then dying on statement_timeout.
Examine the job design: it updates ~40M rows inside a single transaction with no intermediate commits, so locks are held for the job's entire (now multi-hour) duration.
Confirm the trend: batch finish time has crept later week over week as data volume grew, which is why it now spills past 06:00 into business hours.
rootCause: The nightly batch wrapped a huge bulk update in one long transaction that held table locks for its entire runtime. As data volume grew the job ran longer and its end time drifted past the start of business hours, so its long-held locks began blocking live application queries and causing statement timeouts.
resolution: Refactored the job to process in smaller batches with periodic commits (chunked updates) so locks are short-lived, and moved heavy reads to a read replica. Added an earlier start time and a hard runtime guard. App lock-waits dropped to near zero and latency returned to ~150ms even when the job runs.
prevention: Monitor batch job duration and alert if it overruns its window (and if any DB transaction exceeds a max age). Design batch writes in committed chunks to avoid long-held locks, run reporting against replicas, and schedule with headroom that scales as data grows. Add a runtime SLA/kill-switch for the job and dashboards for lock-waits/blocked-query counts so contention is caught immediately.

title: HTTP 429s — Upstream API Rate-Limited the Integration
problem: A feature that calls a third-party shipping/rates API began intermittently failing for users. The integration was receiving HTTP 429 'Too Many Requests' from the upstream provider during busy periods, and the app surfaced the failures instead of handling them.
symptoms: Spikes of 429 responses from the upstream API, clustered around traffic peaks and around a periodic bulk sync. User-facing 'could not fetch shipping rates' errors. Provider response headers showed the rate limit and a Retry-After value the client was ignoring.
logs:
12:31:04 WARN shipping-client received HTTP 429 from api.rates-provider.com
12:31:04 HEADERS X-RateLimit-Limit: 600  X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0  X-RateLimit-Reset: 41  Retry-After: 41
12:31:04 ERROR app surfaced error to user: "shipping rates unavailable"
metric: upstream_429_count=512 in 5m (normally 0); upstream_2xx dropped to 61%
note: our outbound rate ~900 req/min vs provider cap 600 req/min during peak + bulk sync
log: client retries immediately on 429 (no backoff), adding more load -> more 429s
investigationSteps: Identify the failing dependency and status code: errors are HTTP 429 from one specific upstream provider, not internal 5xx — this is rate limiting, not an outage.
Inspect the response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit 600 with Remaining 0 and a Retry-After of 41s shows we are exceeding the provider's documented quota.
Measure our outbound call rate: ~900 req/min against a 600 req/min cap during peaks, especially when a bulk sync overlaps user traffic.
Check client behavior on 429: it retries immediately with no backoff and no Retry-After honoring, which adds load and makes the limiting worse.
Correlate 429 spikes with the bulk sync schedule and traffic peaks to confirm when we breach the quota.
Confirm the fix direction: staying under the cap and honoring Retry-After should eliminate the 429s.
rootCause: The integration sent more requests than the upstream provider's rate limit allowed (especially when a periodic bulk sync overlapped with peak user traffic), and the client ignored the provider's Retry-After/rate-limit headers and retried immediately — so it kept tripping the 429 limit and surfaced the failures to users.
resolution: Implemented client-side throttling to stay under the provider's quota, added retry-with-exponential-backoff that honors the Retry-After header, and added a short-lived cache for rate lookups to cut redundant calls. Rescheduled the bulk sync off-peak. 429s dropped to zero and shipping rates loaded reliably.
prevention: Treat 429 as a first-class, retryable condition: respect Retry-After and rate-limit headers, apply client-side rate limiting/token buckets to stay within quota, and use exponential backoff with jitter (never tight retry loops). Cache idempotent upstream responses, schedule bulk jobs off-peak, request a higher quota if needed, and alert on upstream_429_count and remaining-quota so limits are seen before users are affected.

title: Intermittent HTTP 500s Traced to One Bad Canary Node After Partial Deploy
problem: After a partial (canary) deployment, a small but steady fraction of requests started returning HTTP 500. The errors were intermittent and hard to reproduce because only one of several instances behind the load balancer was bad.
symptoms: Overall 500 error rate sat around ~12% — suspiciously close to 1-in-8, matching one bad instance out of eight. Errors appeared random to users (depended on which backend the LB picked). Healthy instances showed clean logs; one canary instance showed stack traces and a different build SHA.
logs:
lb access log: 500s spread across requests, ~12.4% error ratio overall
per-instance breakdown:
  app-1..app-7 (build a1b2c3) error_rate=0.0%
  app-8       (build f9e8d7, canary) error_rate=99.6%
app-8 log: 13:20:14 ERROR NullPointerException at PricingService.applyDiscount(PricingService.java:88)
app-8 log: 13:20:14 ERROR config key 'discount.tiers' not found (new key, missing on this node's config map)
app-8 readiness: /healthz returns 200 (shallow check) despite failing real requests
metric: requests routed to app-8 ≈ 1/8 of traffic = matches ~12% global 500 rate
investigationSteps: Quantify the error rate: ~12% global 500s is close to 1/8, hinting that one of eight backends is responsible rather than a global regression.
Break errors down per instance (by host/pod label): app-8 is failing ~100% of its requests while app-1..7 are clean — the blast radius is a single node.
Compare build/version: app-8 is running the canary build SHA (f9e8d7); the healthy nodes run the prior build, confirming a partial deploy mismatch.
Read app-8's logs: a NullPointerException in PricingService plus 'config key discount.tiers not found' shows the new build expects config the canary node never received.
Check health probing: app-8's shallow /healthz still returns 200, which is why the LB kept routing real (failing) traffic to it.
Confirm causation: pulling app-8 out of rotation drops the global 500 rate to ~0%, proving the single canary instance was the source.
rootCause: A partial/canary deploy left one instance (app-8) running a new build that required a new config key ('discount.tiers') which was never applied to that node, causing a NullPointerException on nearly every request. Because its health check was shallow (returned 200 regardless), the load balancer kept sending it ~1/8 of traffic, producing intermittent global 500s.
resolution: Immediately removed the bad canary instance from the load-balancer rotation, which dropped the 500 rate to near zero. Then either rolled the canary back or applied the missing config and redeployed it correctly. Made the readiness probe deep enough (a real dependency/config check) so a misconfigured node fails health and is taken out of rotation automatically.
prevention: Use deep readiness/health checks that exercise real dependencies and required config, so a broken node fails out of the LB instead of serving errors. Gate canary deploys on per-instance error-rate SLOs with automatic rollback, version config alongside code (and validate required keys at startup), and add per-instance/per-version error-rate dashboards and alerts so a single bad node is spotted and isolated quickly.
